Several other ships have been targeted in recent weeks, at a time when Russia is intensifying its attacks on Ukraine.]]>

    Production: By Europod, in co-production with Sphera Network.

    EUobserver is proud to have an editorial partnership with Europod to co-publish the podcast series “Briefed” hosted by Léa Marchal. The podcast is available on all major platforms.

    Find the full transcript below: 

    Two ships have been hit by drones in Bulgarian waters in the Black Sea on Monday. Several other ships have been targeted in recent weeks, at a time when Russia is intensifying its attacks on Ukraine.

    So, at what point does a hybrid attack become an attack on Nato? On Monday, two ships were hit by drones in the Bulgarian economic zone in the Black Sea.

    One of them sank, with 11 crew members missing. The second vessel, which belonged to Ukraine, was damaged but did not sink, and all 15 people on board were rescued.

    Read more

    Drone strikes on Black Sea cargo ships point to wider European arc of Russia hybrid threats

    A week earlier, two other cargo ships had been attacked by drones in the same area, killing 10 people. And on 5 October, a Turkish cargo ship carrying grain was sunk by drones shortly after leaving Ukraine.

    There is currently no evidence proving that Russia was behind these attacks, and Moscow has not claimed responsibility.

    But that did not stop Bulgarian Prime Minister Roumen Radev from summoning Russia’s ambassador. Radev said that, while there was no conclusive evidence, the outcome of these attacks clearly benefited Russia more than anyone else.

    Russia’s ambassador to Bulgaria, Eleonora Mitrofanova, said she had received no information from the Russian defence ministry about the attacks. She also suggested that they could have been provocations carried out by a third party.

    And that uncertainty is important, because it makes it much harder for Nato countries to decide when an incident should be treated as an attack.

    Read more

    [Interview] ‘Putin understands only strength’: EU envoy in Kyiv urges stronger air defences and hybrid-war response

    So how do Europeans cope with these attacks? We’ve already seen several Russian drones end up inside EU territory in recent months. And in some cases, they have been clearly identified.

    Take the Russian drone that crashed on a residential building in the Romanian city of Galați in May and injured two people. Or the two drones found at Leipzig airport in Germany this summer, charged with explosives. They were all identified as Russian.

    So far, however, the response has consisted mainly of diplomatic measures and political statements. Neither Bulgaria nor Germany has requested formal consultations under Article 4 of the Nato treaty.

    Article 4 allows a Nato member to ask for consultations when it believes its territorial integrity, political independence or security is threatened.

    Bulgarian Prime Minister Radev has spoken with Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte about the incidents, which are serious enough to be discussed at Nato level. But Bulgaria has not gone as far as triggering Article 4.

    One reason is precisely the ambiguity surrounding all these drone attacks: who is controlling them, whether they were deliberately sent into EU territory, and whether they were jammed or diverted.

    Read more

    Divided EU cyber defence faces real-life Russian and Chinese threats

    But if an attack were clearly attributed to Russia, how would Nato respond? That’s one of the questions currently being discussed within the alliance.

    On Monday, Nato’s top military commander, US General Alexus Grynkewich, said he did not believe a conflict between Russia and Nato was imminent or inevitable.

    But he also presented what Nato calls a “theory of victory”: a plan designed to ensure that the alliance could rapidly neutralise an enemy attacking one of its members.

    The strategy rests on several pillars. One is establishing clear red lines that an adversary should not cross. Another is investing in new military technologies, with drones playing a central role. And the third is maintaining the ability and readiness to fight at short notice.

    The idea is not only to be able to respond if a direct attack happens, but also to deter Russia from continuing what Nato describes as hybrid activities against its members.

      <title>Key US voters say economy is getting worse ahead of midterms, exclusive poll finds</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/oct/15/voters-economy-cost-of-living-prices-poll</link>
      <description><p>Nearly 61% believe country is in recession and 65% of independents say economy is worse, according to new Harris poll</p><ul><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/oct/15/what-is-your-personal-recession-indicator">Tell us: what is your personal ‘recession indicator’?</a></p></li></ul><p>With the midterm elections less than three weeks away, key voting groups including independents, rural voters and even some Republicans are increasingly disenchanted with Donald Trump’s economy, according to an exclusive Harris poll for the Guardian.</p><p>The majority of those surveyed were pessimistic about the economy, with three-quarters of Americans saying they are concerned about a recession while 61% wrongly believe that the US is already experiencing one. By its typical definition, the US is not currently experiencing a recession.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/oct/15/voters-economy-cost-of-living-prices-poll">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <title>US inflation rose to 3.7% in September in blow to Republicans before midterms</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/oct/14/inflation-numbers-september</link>
      <description><p>Final inflation report before voters go to polls comes amid widespread anger over cost of living under Trump</p><ul><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/oct/08/economy-midterm-elections-tell-us">Send us your questions on how the US economy is shaping the midterm elections</a></p></li></ul><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/republicans">Republicans</a> are entering the midterm elections with the highest rate of <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/inflation">inflation</a> since the spring, according to a government report released on Wednesday.</p><p>US price increases reached an annual rate of 3.7%<strong> </strong>in September, according to the latest data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics, up from 3.4% in August. This final inflation report before the pivotal midterm elections comes amid polls showing widespread dissatisfaction with the <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/trump-administration">Trump administration</a> over the cost of living.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/oct/14/inflation-numbers-september">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <title>Bank of America fined $1.2bn for money-laundering failures</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/oct/14/bank-of-america-fined-money-laundering</link>
      <description><p>Third-largest fine in US treasury’s history, due to failure to report suspicious activity, may affect third-quarter earnings</p><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/bank-of-america">Bank of America</a> (BAC.N), has been fined $1.21bn by US regulators for widespread failures to detect ‌potential money laundering and other illicit activity, a penalty the bank said will hurt third-quarter earnings.</p><p>The US treasury department said the fine, the third-largest in department history, is due to the bank’s failure to report more than $5bn in suspicious activity to the government, including $1bn that posed national security-related and other priority illicit finance risks.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/oct/14/bank-of-america-fined-money-laundering">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <description><p>High valuations and debt put sector in danger, while fund also warns on government borrowing and cyber-attacks</p><ul><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/oct/13/imf-global-economy-world-economic-outlook-uk-gdp-forecast-2026">IMF warns global economy ‘could soon test the limits of resilience’</a></p></li></ul><p>The threat of an AI share price crash rippling out across global markets is putting world financial stability at risk, the International Monetary fund has warned.</p><p>In its twice-yearly Global Financial Stability Report, the IMF highlighted the sky-high valuations for AI companies along with their increasing debt pile as one reason that risks in the system are “elevated”.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/oct/13/ai-share-crash-risk-global-imf-debt-corrowing-cyber-attacks">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <description><p>Martin Shkreli’s 2022 release conditions bar him from participating in the pharmaceutical industry, including ownership stakes or business decisions</p><p>The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) and seven US states have alleged that pharmaceutical executive Martin Shkreli repeatedly violated a <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2022/jan/14/martin-shkreli-barred-drug-industry-fined-us-court">lifetime ban</a> on participating in the pharmaceutical industry, and they are asking a judge to hold him in contempt.</p><p>In a <a href="https://www.ftc.gov/news-events/news/press-releases/2026/10/ftc-states-ask-federal-court-hold-martin-shkreli-contempt-allegedly-violating-lifetime">motion </a>filed on Tuesday in US district court in New York City, the FTC and its state co-plaintiffs allege that 43-year-old Shkreli – nicknamed the “Pharma Bro” – has traded stocks in at least 60 pharmaceutical companies and publicly commented on their businesses since his release from prison in May 2022.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/13/martin-shkreli-ftc-ruling-pharma-ban">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/food/2026/oct/15/food-delivery-apps-cost-economy</link>
      <description><p>As Americans use apps like DoorDash and Uber Eats more habitually, they confront the guilt of paying extra fees for convenience</p><ul><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/oct/15/what-is-your-personal-recession-indicator">Tell us: what is your personal ‘recession indicator’?</a></p></li></ul><p>When it comes to food, Caroline Bauldree does not like to “deprive” herself of anything. She does not like to cook either, so that means a lot of food deliveries. “If I want sushi, I’m getting sushi,” said the 24-year-old nanny, who lives in Raleigh, North Carolina. “I’m definitely lazy in that regard.”</p><p>Bauldree got into the habit of near-daily DoorDashing back in college. “I could order whatever food from whatever restaurant and it showed up at my door – that’s the dream,” she said. “But then I just feel like crap about myself because I’m like, ‘wow, I’m a lazy piece of shit.’ Nine times out of 10, I feel bad about myself.”</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/food/2026/oct/15/food-delivery-apps-cost-economy">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <title>Is punishing the poor Trump’s last hand to play?</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/13/trump-aca-healthcare-politics-midterms</link>
      <description><p>The pre-midterm defenestration of ACA enrollees looks like political madness – but the president appears to believe hitting poor people might work for him</p><ul><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/community/live/2026/oct/14/us-economy-affordability-midterm-elections-republicans-trump">Our reporters answer your questions on whether Trump’s economy will sink Republicans in the US midterms</a></p></li></ul><p>There is a manic quality to <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/donaldtrump">Donald Trump</a>’s desperate dash to do something, anything, ahead of November’s <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/us-midterm-elections-2026">midterm elections</a> to convince beleaguered Americans that he can make the pressures his policies have imposed on their livelihoods go away.</p><p>The US president <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/aug/28/trump-cattle-ranchers-beef-imports-backlash">offered</a> to lower barriers against beef imports to limit surging meat prices, only to consider <a href="https://www.politico.com/news/2026/09/23/trump-beef-imports-midterms-gop-panic-01090261">backtracking</a> under <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/aug/25/trump-republican-backlash-beef-tariff-import">pressure</a> from the cow lobby. He <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/sep/22/trump-diesel-export-ban">offered</a> to stop diesel exports, only to find oil companies <a href="https://finance.yahoo.com/energy/articles/market-chatter-us-oil-executives-112235250.html">were</a> <a href="https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/07/chevron-ceo-diesel-export-ban-trump-supply.html">not interested</a>. He weakened fuel efficiency standards, claiming this would trim the price of a new car (and forgetting to point out it will also raise spending on gas). In early October he started mailing <a href="https://www.cnn.com/2026/10/01/economy/trump-obamacare-500-check">$500 checks</a> to nearly a million people touting his healthcare “wins”. Oh, and he promised adult Americans a <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/sep/10/trump-5000-midterm-cash-dividend-response">$5,000 check</a> if Republicans maintain control of Congress. That, too, will <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/sep/10/trump-dividend-republican-midterm-convention">go nowhere</a>.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/13/trump-aca-healthcare-politics-midterms">Continue reading...</a></description>

<![CDATA[Irish Times Feeds]]>https://www.irishtimes.comThu, 15 Oct 2026 23:37:26 +0000en1hourly1<![CDATA[Irish firm with €2.4m debt to Revenue allegedly diverted business to Gibraltar entity, court told]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/crime-law/courts/2026/10/15/irish-firm-with-24m-debt-to-revenue-allegedly-diverted-business-to-gibraltar-entity-court-told/https://www.irishtimes.com/crime-law/courts/2026/10/15/irish-firm-with-24m-debt-to-revenue-allegedly-diverted-business-to-gibraltar-entity-court-told/Thu, 15 Oct 2026 17:49:24 +0000An Irish scaffolding company wound up with debts of almost €2.4 million owed to Revenue has allegedly diverted its business to a Gibraltar-registered entity as part of an attempt to place its assets beyond the reach of creditors, it has been claimed in the High Court.

Adrian García Díaz, a liquidator appointed to Instant Upright Ltd, alleges the company – despite its winding up – has moved customer money to a bank account in the name of a Gibraltar entity, also named Instant Upright Ltd.

This week Judge Brian Cregan granted several reliefs to Bernard Dunleavy, counsel for the liquidator with Keith Farry, including an interim freezing order of the company’s assets.

The judge also granted permission for the liquidator to serve the proceedings on several defendants outside the jurisdiction, including the Gibraltar entity and named individuals the liquidator says are linked to the company.

The individuals are: Robert Stowe, with an address in Monaco, who the liquidator says is 50 per cent beneficial owner of Instant Upright Gibraltar; Andrew James Haynes of Cadiz, Spain, who the liquidator says is also a 50 per cent shareholder; Joseph Oxley of Dubai, who the liquidator says is a company director; Serge Marino of Le Cannet, France, who the liquidator says is a company director; and Graham Donald Croot of Melbourne, Australia, who the liquidator says is a company director.

Reporting on the proceedings was restricted for 48 hours to allow time for the liquidator’s lawyers in Gibraltar to make an application to the courts there for an equivalent freezing order.

In a sworn statement Díaz said he was seeking the freezing orders in circumstances where there was “a real and substantial risk” the defendants will “dissipate, conceal or remove” money in the bank account held in the Gibraltar company’s name beyond the liquidator’s reach.

Díaz said he was appointed as liquidator over the company by court order in January, following a petition by the Revenue Commissioners. He said the company is also indebted to the ESB in the sum of €30,831, RFC Security Ltd for €43,405, and Korea South East Power Co Ltd for €2.9 million.

The liquidator said he sought to obtain information from Instant Upright directors about the company’s affairs but no response was received.

The case will return next week.

]]>Richard Newstead<![CDATA[Global stocks edge lower as AI and rate fears hit tech]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/15/global-stocks-edge-lower-as-ai-and-rate-fears-hit-tech/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/15/global-stocks-edge-lower-as-ai-and-rate-fears-hit-tech/Thu, 15 Oct 2026 17:03:11 +0000Global equity markets edged lower on Thursday as concerns about artificial intelligence (AI) spending and higher interest rates fuelled a continued sell-off in technology and chip stocks.

Investors have been unnerved by ​valuations of companies in the AI sector as more voices question the sustainability of demand for data centres.

On Wall Street, the tech-heavy Nasdaq was down and the Philadelphia SE Semiconductor index was down 2 per cent. The benchmark S&P 500 reversed losses in early trade and was trading higher led by healthcare and materials stocks while the Dow was up ​1 per cent.

Dublin

Kenmare Resources, the Dublin-listed titanium minerals miner, saw its shares rise 3.7 per cent despite downgrading its production forecasts for the year. The company is the subject of a potential bid by a company controlled by the Abu Dhabi royal family.

Ryanair enjoyed a 1.5 per cent bounce in its shares – they closed at €22.43 – as oil prices slipped. The rise came even though the EU’s top court ruled regulators must take the limit of 32 million passengers at Dublin Airport into account when allocating take-off and landing slots to airlines there.

Airlines, including Ryanair, had challenged the Irish Aviation Authority’s decision to take the cap into account when allocating slots for winter 2024 at the airport, prompting the High Court to refer the matter to the Court of Justice of the European Union.

Bank of Ireland and AIB were down 1.2 per cent and 0.8 per cent respectively amid speculation that central banks globally will raise interest rates again before Christmas, a move that might dampen borrowing.

Europe

In European equity markets, the CAC 40 in Paris ended up 0.8 per cent, while the DAX 40 in Frankfurt added 0.3 per cent.

In Frankfurt, semiconductor firm Infineon lost 4.8 per cent. Siemens Energy, which provides power solutions to data centres, shed 2.6 per cent, both well above earlier lows.

]]>Provision<![CDATA[The rich are getting richer, so why no wealth tax?]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/15/the-rich-are-getting-richer-so-why-no-wealth-tax/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/15/the-rich-are-getting-richer-so-why-no-wealth-tax/Thu, 15 Oct 2026 12:03:13 +0000Around the world, the rich are getting richer, with soaring stock markets and other asset values lining their pockets. So why – in most countries – is there no wealth tax?

True, most tax systems do tax wealth in specific ways, such as charges on property or capital gains. But straight-up wealth taxes – an annual charge on the value of the assets held – are rare.

But with exchequers worldwide searching for cash, taxing wealth is coming back on to the agenda. A new report from the Economic and Social Research Institute (ESRI) crunches the numbers and outlines the key choices facing Irish policymakers.

It shows there is a lot of wealth in Ireland that could be taxed, but raising a significant amount of money requires big political decisions.

For Ireland, as for other countries, the choice is whether a wealth tax would be for show – a political signal that the wealthiest should pay a bit more – or for dough, in other words to raise a significant amount of money for the exchequer.

Higher wealth – fewer wealth taxes

One of the peculiarities of recent years is that although the wealth of the billionaire class has risen worldwide, the number of countries with wealth taxes has shrunk.

The ESRI report points out that 12 European countries levied an annual tax on net wealth in 1990 compared with only Norway, Spain and Switzerland last year.

Low revenue yields, administrative challenges and concerns that capital would move to other countries are among the reasons cited for countries abandoning the taxes.

France abolished its wealth tax in 2018, citing fears of wealth moving out of the country, and replaced it with a tax on real estate worldwide assets valued at more than €1.3 million. Despite rising wealth, the key message is that full-scale wealth taxes are not easy to design and implement.

Wealth in Ireland

Household wealth in Ireland, as measured by the Central Statistics Office household finance and consumption survey in 2023, was €927 billion, about two-and-a-half-times higher than a decade earlier.

That is an average (median) net wealth of just under €256,000 per household, with the family home the main asset for the vast majority. Where a mortgage is still outstanding, this is subtracted from the net wealth figures.

The story of Irish assets over the past decade can be told in a few headlines – rising house prices are the key factor, followed by lower household debt as the Celtic Tiger loans are paid down and a rise in business assets among the better off.

The top 10 per cent still controls close to 50 per cent of wealth. It is worth noting, also, that separate Central Bank of Ireland data, which showed wealth at just over €1 billion early 2023 – a bit higher than the CSO – estimated it at being more than €1.42 billion in the first quarter of this year.

Taxing questions

Assets are taxed in Ireland via a few routes, notably capital gains tax and capital acquisitions tax on inheritance and gifts.

However, even if you add the amounts collected via these taxes to stamp duty and local property tax – which operates more like a charge – the total revenue comes to less than €6 billion in 2025 out of total tax revenue of more than €105 billion. Could a wealth tax increase the revenue significantly?

Well, it depends. The key insight from the ESRI paper was that if an Irish wealth tax was going to raise significant money, then it would have to have a wide base – in other words most assets would have to be included. If this happened, then even if the tax kicked in at relatively high wealth levels, significant sums could be raised.

The political problem is that a broad base takes in areas such as businesses, farms and the family home. If all wealth in the State were taxed at 1 per cent, the yield would be €9.3 billion based on the 2023 figures and probably more than €10 billion now. This is not a realistic scenario, but it provides a kind of benchmark.

The researchers go through a range of scenarios, with the widest possible tax base, one excluding the family home and a narrow definition including mainly financial assets and investment property. Cut-off points above which wealth would be taxed range from €250,000 to €2 million, with these figures doubled for a married couple. In all cases the tax rate is 1 per cent and pensions are excluded.

Three lessons

The first – and most striking – lesson is the importance of the range of assets covered. Exempting the family home, businesses and farms cuts the pot significantly.

At a threshold of €500,000 for example – which would be €1 million for a married couple – a narrow base just including financial assets and other investments would raise less than €450 million annually, while one including all assets would raise close to €3 billion.

The second lesson is not surprising: it is that as the threshold lowers for the wealth level where the tax kicks in, the numbers rise sharply.

At the €500,000 threshold, 4.5 per cent of households have to pay. At the lowest one, €250,000, it rises to more than a third. But the share of total national wealth rises less sharply – from 19 per cent to 32 per cent – as the amount of assets held per household falls sharply at lower levels.

The third lesson reflects the importance of the family home as the source of wealth for middle and higher earners. The main residence is only a small portion of wealth at the very highest level – where households typically own businesses or have significant financial asset. For middle Ireland, the family home is the key asset.

For a wealth tax covering everyone with assets over €250,000, exempting the family home would cut the annual tax take from €4.5 billion to €2.6 billion.

Who pays?

The profile of those who pay depends crucially on the rules set. The wealthiest top 10 per cent will always be hit hardest, but a key political decision would be where to draw the line. Too high and you limit the revenue raised. Too low and it ends up as a family home tax on middle earners.

The fact that there are wealthy people with relatively low incomes is another complication.

Overall, an Irish wealth tax would mainly hit middle-aged and older property owners – those aged 55 years of age plus would pay about two-thirds of the tax under most scenarios. If the base of the tax is narrow – excluding the family home – then those aged 65 or more would be in the firing line as those hold higher investments in savings and other financial assets.

They would typically paying close to half or more of the total tax, depending on the rules. On the flip side, younger renters hold hardly any wealth, so would pay little tax.

The bottom line

The report underlines that a wealth tax could raise a significant sum in revenue, but only if it covered a broad base of wealth.

This brings politically sensitive areas of business and farm wealth and the family home into the picture – all advantaged by the Irish tax system at present. An alternative, as recommended by the Commission on Tax and Welfare in 2023, is to increase existing taxes on wealth rather that introducing a separate new wealth tax.

But there is no easy decisions either here for Irish politicians – do they, for example, end the favourable inheritance rules for businesses and farms? Or hike local property tax?

None of these things will happen for as long as there is a budget surplus. But with the Irish Fiscal Advisory Council warning that more revenue will be needed in the years ahead to meet the costs of an ageing population and climate change, sooner or later Irish policymakers will have to consider where it comes from.

Sinn Féin has called for a study on a wealth tax and recommended hikes on capital taxes and pensions. Labour’s alternative budget also calls for a hike in a range of capital taxes, including capital gains tax and the capital acquisitions tax.

The Social Democrats want to tax the “super-wealthy”, likely only to work as part of an international drive in this area, while People Before Profit also want to “tax the multi-millionaires.”

But more taxes on wealth are now creeping on to the Irish political agenda. The comfortable classes are in the firing line – even if they don’t realise it yet.

]]>Imen Ben Youssef<![CDATA[The global economy and the art of living dangerously]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/economy/2026/10/15/the-global-economy-and-the-art-of-living-dangerously/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/economy/2026/10/15/the-global-economy-and-the-art-of-living-dangerously/Thu, 15 Oct 2026 13:30:00 +0000The past few days have reminded us of one of the two chief contemporary economic realities: the president of the US is a wrecker.

Yet this is consistent with the other reality, which is that despite the disruptions and shocks of our era, the world economy remains a powerful growth machine, driven by remarkable innovations, risk-taking finance and large accumulations of debt. Can this last?

The reason for believing it will is that growth has been the dominant feature of the global economy since the middle of the last century. Yet we must always remember that growth is one thing, but stable growth quite another.

What, then, is the latest US president Donald Trump outrage? First, he started a war on Iran, without a plan, which has raised diesel prices in the US and worldwide. Then, a few days ago, he made a deal with Vladimir Putin to release Russian diesel on global markets, in violation of sanctions imposed after Putin’s illegal invasion of Ukraine.

Trump also told Kyiv to halt its strikes on Russian oil refineries and threatened to cut off intelligence sharing with Ukraine and access to US-made weapons.

This “deal” is both foolish and wicked: foolish, because it is too small to lower diesel prices significantly, and wicked, because it is prepared to sacrifice a country that is struggling heroically to be free from tyranny.

Current US policymaking is not just reckless and immoral. It is also one of the causes of the world’s unpredictability.

Thus, the International Monetary Fund’s (IMF) latest World Economic Outlook (WEO) starts with the following comment from Silvana Tenreyro, the new economic counsellor: “In less than seven years, the global economy has been subjected to an exceptional sequence of events.”

Current US policymaking is not just reckless and immoral. It is also one of the causes of the world’s unpredictability.

Yet all but one of these shocks, the exception being the pandemic, are man-made, or perhaps “strongman-made”. The others are the war in Ukraine, the tariff war and the war in the Middle East. Putin launched the first of these in 2022. Trump, of course, began the other two.

These shocks have, as Tenreyro says, “tested the resilience of households, firms, financial markets and governments. Individually, each of these big developments would have been considered unlikely. Their confluence over such a short period of time is even more extraordinary.”

Yet, remarkably, the WEO’s forecasts for growth this year and next, at 3.1 and 3.4 per cent respectively, are “broadly unchanged from April”, despite more persistent energy disruption than was then expected.

Global inflation is, however, expected to hit 4.7 per cent this year, as a result of higher commodity prices, and 4.1 per cent in 2027. But, happily, “the pass-through to core inflation is expected to be limited”.

The explanations for this resilience are familiar. They include adjustment of exports and imports away from direct trade between the US and China. More recently, however, the dominant factors have been the flexibility of the global energy economy, discussed here last week, and the investment boom triggered by artificial intelligence (AI).

Yet neither is guaranteed to last. As Nick Butler points out, stocks of crude and products are low after six months of drawdowns. Moreover, “product exports of diesel and jet fuel [from the Gulf] remain minimal”. Also at risk are supplies of naphtha, urea and liquefied natural gas (the latter of special importance to Europe).

The AI investment boom also concentrates risk. Even if AI itself works out, the level of investment is likely to stop growing, if not decline, at some point. Moreover, AI might not work out financially on the hoped-for scale at all.

Other fragilities are evident, notably the fiscal positions. Despite the big post-pandemic rise in real and nominal interest rates, most large economies continue to run significant primary fiscal deficits (before interest payments).

It would help if the shocks stopped, too. Alas, given our leaders, I would not bet on that.

The US position stands out, with a forecast primary fiscal deficit of 4.8 per cent of gross domestic product (GDP) this year, a share of T-bill issuance in gross borrowing at 58 per cent and an average maturity of a mere 5.9 years.

The WEO rightly emphasises the importance of rebuilding fiscal space. The good news is that, in today’s circumstances, the negative impact of structural fiscal tightening is likely to be offset by lower real and nominal interest rates. But redressing global current accounts imbalances will also be essential. That must, at last, involve China.

Ireland is richer and spending more than 30 years ago but is it making us happy?

The WEO emphasises other downside risks, including a worsening of the ongoing wars, (probably AI-enhanced) cyber threats and climate catastrophes.

Neither a stock market crash nor a collapse in AI-related investment can be ruled out, should returns on AI disappoint. Upside economic risks include still faster progress with AI technology, though that could also inflict devastating social consequences.

Another plausible upside is an accelerated energy transition, as recent events underline the unreliability of fossil fuels. Given their physical location, these are bound to remain so for many countries.

John FitzGerald: Budget reversal of policy on tackling climate change was a mistake

The WEO notes that the ability to exploit AI and meet energy needs reliably will be crucial for growth prospects. Sadly, the world’s poorest countries are particularly vulnerable in both respects. Thus, the WEO rightly fears that their living standards are likely to fall still farther behind those in richer countries.

It would be good to believe the world will become less prone to shocks. But it will probably not do so. The best response is to strengthen fundamentals, notably economic flexibility and dynamism, together with energy resilience. In this context, as the WEO notes, it is essential to make support for people vulnerable to shocks targeted and temporary.

In 1996, consumers in Ireland were experiencing a clear improvement in employment, incomes, migration and inflation following the trying times of the 1980s but today sentiment is affected by markedly higher living costs, infrastructure constraints and concerns about Ireland’s exposure to international policy changes against a backdrop of geopolitical instability and persistent economic shocks.

“The past 30 years have seen Ireland build a hugely successful economy, but this has not automatically translated to an increase in consumer confidence,” said economist Austin Hughes. “The sentiment survey suggests that living through periods of boom and bust has made Irish consumers focus more on persistent day-to-day pressures, rather than on wealth that might not be permanent.”

]]>Douglas Rissing<![CDATA[People don’t leave jobs, they leave bad managers. What makes a great one?]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/work/2026/10/15/what-makes-a-great-manager-researchers-have-been-working-hard-to-find-out/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/work/2026/10/15/what-makes-a-great-manager-researchers-have-been-working-hard-to-find-out/Thu, 15 Oct 2026 05:00:00 +0000When you think back over your career, which manager do you remember first? The boss who believed in you and gave you opportunities or the manager who thwarted and belittled you at every turn?

The managerial personality traits and behaviours we observe early in our careers often shape our own management style later. If we liked a boss, we might try to emulate what they did well while avoiding the more negative behaviours of someone we considered a bad leader or a toxic colleague.

In Ireland, many people who are promoted to manager never receive any training on how to manage or even know what good looks like. On a Monday, they’re a colleague and on Tuesday, they’re the boss.

To figure out how to behave as a manager, they might do a little detective work to determine what style is preferred at their company. If Mary was promoted for hitting her targets every month – regardless of staff burnout levels – then that might be someone they choose as a role model.

Or they might look higher up the ladder to the chief executive. If that person is a strong communicator who motivates the team with a clear vision and regular updates then they might choose to focus on developing these behaviours first.

Organisations that value sustainable growth and efficiency should never leave managerial expectations to chance. The cost of this oversight is high when it comes to employee engagement, turnover and productivity.

People don’t leave jobs, they leave bad managers.

Managerial skills continue to be a gap in Ireland, with 61 per cent of HR professionals surveyed identifying insufficient line manager capability and capacity as the top constraint, according to the CIPD Ireland’s HR Practices in Ireland 2026.

According to Gallup, half of resigning employees cite their manager as the reason they’re leaving. That’s not surprising considering that so much of your compensation, growth opportunities and motivation come from interactions with your manager. This relationship – good or bad – correlates directly with employee engagement.

Employees who leave because of their manager say poor communication, lack of recognition, micromanagement, favouritism and unfairness are the top reasons the relationship breaks down. Companies spend significant sums on hiring employees and training them in only to fail them when it comes to training up their managers.

Thankfully, decades of research on managerial prowess show us what good looks like when it comes to being an effective manager. Academics have identified a set of core traits and behaviours that distinguish effective managers from ineffective ones.

An effective manager is able to integrate certain personality traits (especially conscientiousness, extroversion and openness), interpersonal behaviours (communication, caring, trust building and ethical leadership) and decision-making competence with a people-oriented style.

Individuals like this outperform those who focus on a task-oriented approaches – hitting targets, getting through the to-do list – across most contexts studied.

This ties in with what workers say they value most at work. European workers put a safe environment for mental and physical health (71 per cent) and a trusting environment (69 per cent) ahead of good pay and benefits (66 per cent), according to Eurofound’s European Working Conditions Survey 2024.

A beginner’s guide to the 9-5 work week: Minimise your morning, don’t overshare

Are managers born or made? How many times have you heard “she’s a born leader” or “he really gets results”?

We assume that certain personality traits or behaviours automatically lead to promotion but research shows they might not be the things that make a manager truly effective. And that’s good news for introverts, more reflective personality types or those who’ve always thought, or felt, they’re not manager material.

An influential study in Personnel Psychology entitled Trait and Behavioural Theories of Leadership, led by Scott DeRue in 2011, was one of the first to explore which useful traits and effective behaviours worked best for managers. Over time, more studies have confirmed and built on their findings.

The most effective behaviours are a mix of transformational, task-oriented, relations-oriented, and change-oriented rather than a single universal style. Within those behaviours, problem-solving stands out as a particularly strong predictor of managerial effectiveness. The good news is that many of these behaviours can be taught and developed.

Managers who are perceived to be extroverts – or who fit stereotypical traits of what a leader looks or sounds like – have a definite advantage when it comes to getting the job but research shows that once they’re in the job, it’s behaviours such as agreeableness and emotional stability that help managers succeed in the role.

Unfortunately, organisations often promote people who put themselves forward or who excel at the technical aspects of the job, then just hope that their managerial skills miraculously emerge afterwards. Research suggests that such an approach can backfire, and that manager quality has a measurable effect on team results.

People who self-select into management perform worse than randomly assigned managers, according to a small study by Ben Weidmann and colleagues in the Quarterly Journal of Economics last year. Selecting managers on their skills rather than desire to lead could substantially improve organisational performance, according to the findings.

Effective leadership appears to depend less on who looks or sounds like a leader than on the behaviours and skills they actually demonstrate. The most influential studies on effective managers have a clear answer: behaviours and skills matter more than demographics or personality traits.

If you’re a new manager, or even a seasoned one, here are some top tips based on research that shows which behaviours have the greatest positive impact.

  1. Make your expectations crystal clear: Agree specific, measurable goals with each individual so they know what success looks like from the start. Don’t make them waste time guessing what you need and want; just tell them.
  2. Give feedback little and often: Specific, timely comments and public recognition of positive contributions are among the most impactful behaviours for a manager. Team members need encouragement to feel motivated and it helps them know they’re progressing in the right direction.
  3. Listen actively, then act: People need to feel heard and valued. Working on your active listening skills – such as maintaining eye contact and not interrupting – build trust. Make sure you take notes of the conversation and follow through on what was agreed. Visible follow-through builds credibility and employee loyalty.
  4. Focus on the person, not just the role: Nobody wants to feel like they’re just a number, a key performance indicator (KPI) or a job description. Managers need to take time getting to know each team member and help them play to their strengths. Employees rank most highly managers who show care for them as individuals.
  5. Maintain an open-door policy: Managers’ availability and approachability are linked to higher levels of trust. Although you don’t have to physically keep your door ajar, you need to ensure staff know they can talk to you about most things at any time.
  6. Be fair: Integrity, fairness and humility predict trust and effectiveness.
  7. Manage yourself first: Self-awareness and emotional steadiness are what make managers effective, not just visible.
  8. Learn from peers: When you take on a role as a manager, lean on mentors and peers to help you increase learning quickly so these new skills stick.

Margaret E Ward is chief executive of Clear Eye, a leadership consultancy. margaret@cleareye.ie

]]>Thierry Monasse<![CDATA[Will I inherit my sister-in-law’s share of the family home?]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/15/will-i-inherit-my-sister-in-laws-share-of-the-family-home/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/15/will-i-inherit-my-sister-in-laws-share-of-the-family-home/Thu, 15 Oct 2026 04:00:00 +0000Question

My husband inherited part of his family home, along with his sister and brother. His sister has the right to live there. She has a disability and is older than them.

It is likely that she will either go into residential care or will pass away before her brothers do.

In her will, she gives money to her nieces, nephews and to a couple of charities and friends. The rest goes to her two brothers and me.

What happens to her share of the house if she moves into residential care or if she dies before me or her two brothers?

Answer

The three siblings have been left the house as “tenants in common”, the will says. This means each owns an equal one-third share, says Helen Ferguson, solicitor and partner in the private client department at Mason Hayes & Curran.

This differs from “joint ownership”, where if one of the siblings were to die, their share would automatically pass to the other two – and so forth, to one owner.

“As these siblings are tenants in common, as and when each of them dies, their one-third share passes to their estate, not to the other surviving owners,” says Ferguson.

The will says the sister has the right to live in the property for life. But this wording is a bit redundant, says Ferguson. It is probably more of an expression of the parents’ wish for how things would go, she says.

“If you own a property as a tenant in common, you have an automatic right to live there for your period of ownership anyway,” says Ferguson. “So, any one of the three of them has the right to live there, actually.

“What the will doesn’t say is that the sister has an ‘exclusive right’ to live there. That would mean she had a ‘life interest’ which would postpone the legal ownership of her brothers,” says Ferguson.

“Because it doesn’t say ‘exclusive’, the other two have an equal right to live there if they want.”

This doesn’t mean that a nephew could just move into the property, for example.

“He is not an owner. I think that would need the consent of the other co-owners,” says Ferguson.

So, what happens to the house if the sister goes into residential care? The three siblings could agree to rent it out, with any profits split in three equal shares. Or the three could agree that a family member moves in as a caretaker.

Alternatively, if the three of them agree to it, the house could be sold.

There are some important things for the siblings to consider sooner rather than later.

“If one of them was to lose their mental capacity to make decisions, then you have a problem because you have a co-owner who cannot sign a contract or take a decision,” says Ferguson.

If there are concerns about the older sister, for example, and she still has mental capacity, talk to her about enduring power of attorney, Ferguson advises.

This is a legal document set up while you have full mental capacity to choose someone you trust, called your attorney, to manage your financial, property and/or personal affairs should you ever lose the capacity to do so yourself in the future.

“If she does that, then she has appointed someone in her place to sell the property, if they all decide that is the right thing to do,” says Ferguson.

If she did lose mental capacity and money was needed to pay for her residential care, for example, but an enduring power of attorney had not been arranged, her brothers would have to apply to court for a decision-making representative to be appointed for her.

Getting an enduring power of attorney in place now will be less time-consuming and expensive.

If the sister were to die before her brothers, her one-third share goes into her estate, to be administered in accordance with her will.

“If she has enough cash to pay the legacies she has made to the nieces, nephews, friends and charities mentioned in her will, then her share of the house would form part of the residue of her estate,” says Ferguson.

This residue is the part the sister says she wants to go to her brothers and sister-in-law. But money left as a legacy in a will takes priority over anything left in the residue – legacies get paid first.

So, if she didn’t have enough cash to pay the legacies, then eventually her one-third share of the house would have to be sold to fund the legacies, says Ferguson.

“The legacies have to be paid at some stage, and the executors won’t want to wait until everyone on the property title has died.

“The executors will look for agreement from the owners to sell the property to pay the legacies, or if the brothers wanted to keep the property, then they would have to fund those legacies.”

If the sister dies, will her sister-in-law, the reader, inherit her one-third share of the property?

Not exactly, says Ferguson.

“If the sister specifically left her share of the house to her sister-in-law, then that would take priority over the money legacies, but if she doesn’t, then whatever cash is there would first be used to pay the legacies and expenses,” says Ferguson.

If the reader’s husband dies, leaving everything to her in his will, then the reader will inherit his one-third share of the house. If he dies without a will, then two-thirds of his estate, including the house, would go to his wife and one-third to his children.

The name of the reader who submitted the question is not being published to protect the identities of those involved.

]]><![CDATA[Ikea is coming for your unwanted furniture – and your wallet]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/14/ikea-is-coming-for-your-unwanted-furniture-and-your-wallet/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/14/ikea-is-coming-for-your-unwanted-furniture-and-your-wallet/Wed, 14 Oct 2026 04:00:00 +0000How many Ikea items do you have in your home? For the 65 per cent of Irish adults who say they have at least one, the launch last week of a new second-hand online marketplace here by the Swedish giant will be good news.

Irish fans of the world’s biggest furniture retailer are legion. Its Ballymun shop was its best performing store globally in 2023, with some 3.2 million customers walking through the door. Total retail sales here reached €247.3 million last year, with Irish customers buying more of Ikea’s moving boxes and red wine glasses than any other country in the world.

Now, you will be able to flog your old Ikea furniture and buy preloved items on the cheap through the retailer too. So how will it work, can you make money, why is Ikea doing it – and during this Climate Action Week, is it really any good for the environment?

New marketplace

The launch of Ikea’s second-hand marketplace means customers who have signed up to the company’s Ikea Family membership scheme can connect to buy and sell pre-owned Ikea items locally. Think eBay, Vinted or Facebook Marketplace – but only for Ikea goods.

The new digital second-hand shop will make it easier for people to make some money from old Ikea furniture they no longer need, while helping others to find discounted, pre-owned items, including those no longer available in stores, says Ikea.

The only things you can’t resell are kitchen accessories, mattresses and food.

The launch here follows successful trials by the Swedish company of online second-hand marketplaces in Spain, Norway, Portugal, Poland, Sweden and Belgium.

In those countries, demand has been strongest for bedroom furniture, storage solutions and livingroom sofas and chairs. The company’s Kallax storage cubes and its Malm chest of drawers have emerged as two of the most popular items being traded second-hand to date.

Items are being listed for less than half of their full retail price, says Ikea.

“When we look at the average reduction in price for items listed, it’s 60 per cent or less,” says Greg Lucas, sustainability manager, Ikea UK and Ireland.

Got your eye on the popular Malm Storklinta chest of six drawers? These had been retailing new this summer for €160; now you could nab a set second-hand and in good nick for just €96.

That Besta TV unit that was retailing for €255? If the retailer’s predictions are correct, you could now secure a preloved model from another Ikea Family member for about €100.

Ikea has already cut its prices on about 1,500 products by between 15 and 25 per cent in 20 European countries, including Ireland, since September 1st. The move was an attempt by the flat-pack furniture retailer to counter the cost-of-living crisis as consumer confidence continues to remain depressed.

So, if you are selling products second-hand that you bought before the price drop, you may not recoup quite so much of your original spend.

Selling and buying

Unlike some second-hand marketplaces, sellers on Ikea’s site can sell for free, at least for now. Selling through some competing third-party sites can attract fees.

For example, a second-hand Ikea Kallax for sale in Ireland on Vinted right now is priced at €25, but a fee of €1.95 is charged to “cover the cost of providing a safe smooth experience for our community”, says Vinted.

Posting a product for sale on the Ikea site is arguably easier too. Sellers simply tick the product they are selling from Ikea’s vast library, and their ad will pre-populate with the exact description and dimensions, with links to spare parts. Some small spare parts are free. Sellers can also post photos of the item they have taken themselves.

“It’s down to the buyer to highlight what condition it’s in today,” says Lucas.

Helpfully, buyers can post reviews of sellers too, which should help to keep community members honest.

You can choose to receive payment by bank transfer or opt for an Ikea digital refund card – which will give sellers a 15 per cent bonus.

Sellers accepting payment via the refund card can use the credit against new Ikea products. You can also use it to buy other second-hand products in store through the company’s Buyback and Resell service.

The pleasures of Vinted have often little to do with money, although the cash is nice

This service enables customers to sell eligible products back to Ikea in exchange for in-store credit. By enabling this, Ikea may be countering criticism that the 15 per cent bonus incentivises us back into the shop to buy yet more new stuff on a planet on which there is already too much stuff.

You can also use the card to buy food at Ikea.

When an item is purchased, payment is held securely by Ikea’s payment service provider until the buyer has collected or received the item and confirms acceptance through the marketplace. At that point, a 48-hour buyer protection period begins.

During this period, the buyer can raise an issue if the product does not match its listing. For example, buyers can contact support if there are missing parts, undisclosed damage, or if the item is not an authentic Ikea product.

If there are no issues, payment is automatically released to the seller.

If there is an issue, the payment remains on hold while a refund request is reviewed in line with the marketplace’s buyer protection policy. Ikea says it can support dispute resolution where needed.

While there are no fees on the Irish site for now, the company has introduced a “buyer protection fee” in Spain, which it says supports “safeguards”, like ensuring only authentic Ikea products in usable condition are advertised and only by Ikea Family members.

Delivery

Sellers and buyers will have to arrange delivery and/or pickup between themselves. But with Ikea products so ubiquitous in Irish homes, you probably won’t have a hard time finding a Billy bookcase or Kallax cube near you.

Indeed, after just 10 years in the State, some 65 per cent of Irish adults say they have at least one Ikea product in their home, according to research the company published in July 2019 to mark that 10th anniversary.

One in four people in Ireland surveyed said that Ikea was their go-to when moving into a new home, with another 21 per cent saying they visited the furniture giant when planning their first home with their partner. Some 70 per cent of Irish parents said they had Ikea products in their home.

Despite the lack of a delivery service, buying second-hand could prove more convenient than buying new. Finding a good-as-new Poang chair for sale in your own town will spare you the schlep to Ballymun, where a tour of the gargantuan shop has been known to test the most solid of relationships.

What Irish shoppers love to buy in Ikea

Ikea says it is “exploring” a “convenient, affordable and sustainable” delivery service for bulky items, says Lucas.

It piloted the use of TipTapp in Sweden and Lisbon this summer. This is a peer-to-peer mobile app that matches people who need help moving or delivering items with people who have a car and spare time.

“Once the Ikea online marketplace purchase is completed, the buyer can post a ‘delivery task’, set the price they are prepared to pay for delivery and receive offers from available ‘helpers’,” says Ikea.

They can compare helper ratings and reviews, choose a helper, track delivery in real time and pay securely once the item arrives. For those who just can’t wait for that Poang chair, collection and delivery may even be available on the same day.

Ikea’s timing in Ireland is something to behold. Maybe it’s not so much the Scandi-inspired aesthetic that resonates with us so much as its ability to meet the moment. And we’ve had our moments.

Ikea opened its big blue Lego-like superstore in Dublin 11 in 2009 at the height of Ireland’s financial crash. Yes, its furniture was mass-produced and everywhere, but it was also affordable at a time when roughly 150,000 mortgage borrowers had plunged into negative equity, according to estimates from the Economic and Social Research Institute think tank, with house prices dropping from their early-2007 peak.

The higher-end furniture retailer Habitat had shut up shop in Dublin and Galway in 2008 due, it said, to a “severe” deterioration in sales.

‘Vinted is a wolf in sheep’s clothing’: Ireland’s vintage stores on facing down online challenges

Now, almost 20 years on from the crash, we find ourselves punch-drunk from another cost-of-living crisis and an ongoing housing crisis, and with further economic clouds scrambling on the horizon. The launch of Ikea’s second-hand selling website here on the day Budget 2027 was unveiled is well timed, or portentous.

Being able to furnish your entire home and garden affordably and from one retailer, using new or second-hand products, is not to be sniffed at. Even if everyone in your estate has the same Billy bookcase.

Slice of the pie

Second-hand shopping has become big business, and Ikea knows it. It has emerged as a “quiet but significant shift” in Irish consumer behaviour, according to analysis by RedC.

It’s no longer a niche trend confined to charity shops, vintage enthusiasts or bargain hunters. Increasingly, it is becoming a normal part of everyday consumer behaviour in Ireland, says RedC.

It’s not just a way to save money but part of a broader move towards more sustainable and circular patterns of consumption. Second-hand shopping is becoming an established part of life here.

Brands are having to rethink how they compete in a world where new products increasingly sit alongside refurbished, reused and preloved alternatives.

More than nine in 10 adults in Ireland say they shop for second-hand goods, according to research commissioned by Ikea in September. Some 45 per cent of adults said they buy pre-owned furniture.

Are you a fool to pay full price? From paint to phones, buying second-hand can slash your costs

No doubt Ikea has been watching established second-hand marketplaces like eBay, Facebook Marketplace and Vinted steal its Swedish meatball lunch. Those platforms are full of listings of second-hand Ikea items, likely hitting sales of new Ikea products while returning nothing to the retailer.

So now, Ikea is getting in on the act. By launching its own second-hand marketplace here, it is harvesting something back from this thriving second-hand market of its own products. By incentivising payment through an Ikea digital refund card, money from transacting its products second-hand gets directed back to Ikea.

But is it green?

Buying second hand is great, says the Rediscovery Centre, the National Centre for the Circular Economy, but buying less overall, and repairing what you have, is better.

“The bigger challenge is that, in Ireland, we simply consume too much,” says Claire Downey, chief executive of the Rediscovery Centre, which is headquartered just over a kilometre from Ikea’s Ballymun outlet.

Irish homes contain an average of €531 worth of unused home and garden furniture, according to Ikea’s research, and unused home decor and accessories worth an average of €347. Yikes.

That baby changing table you bought new, and used only for a few short years, could have been borrowed.

“Many of the things we buy are not needed for long. Borrowing, sharing and renting are great alternatives to buying and they help to reduce the amount of stuff we accumulate in the first place, as well as saving money and space in our homes,” says Downey.

Ikea’s tantalising promise is that we are all just one good shoe rack away from nirvana

Circular.ie and Repairmystuff.ie are digital platforms that support communities to reduce consumption and waste by sharing, reusing and repairing, she says.

Many of the things we spend money replacing could easily be repaired, says Downey.

“We’d love to see a shift in mindset where people automatically consider repairing, renting and borrowing, or buying second-hand before buying new.”

]]>Ikea

   <description>Lachs gilt wegen seiner Omega-3-Fettsäuren als gesundes Lebensmittel, entsprechend stetig steigt die Nachfrage nach dem Fisch. Europas größte Lachsfarmen in Norwegen beginnen nun damit, ihre Fische mit Hühnenabfällen zu füttern, und brechen damit ein Tabu auf der Suche nach billigen Produktionsmitteln. <item rdf:about="https://orf.at/stories/3445157/">
   <title>Junge verletzen sich besonders häufig</title>
   <description>Der Fitnessboom geht mit einem deutlichen Anstieg der Verletzungen beim Kraftsport einher. 2025 mussten rund 3.300 Menschen nach Unfällen beim Krafttraining in Spitälern behandelt werden, teilte das Kuratorium für Verkehrssicherheit (KFV) am Donnerstag mit. Besonders betroffen sind junge Menschen: 52 Prozent der Verletzten waren zwischen 15 und 29 Jahre alt. Rund drei Viertel sind Männer. Am häufigsten kam es zu Muskel- und Sehnenverletzungen.</description>

The Ukrainian Institute of National Remembrance (UINR) has reported the discovery of 30 human remains at a site in Poland where Polish partisans killed Ukrainian civilians during World War Two.

The head of the UINR, Oleksandr Alfyorov, thanked Poland for granting permission to conduct research at the location, which he said would help advance “true reconciliation” between the two countries over their difficult shared history.

Ukraine has likewise recently allowed Poland to search for and exhume the remains of Poles massacred by Ukrainian nationalists during the war.

At the end of August, the Polish authorities approved a request from Ukraine to conduct a search in the village of Łasków in southeastern Poland, around 10km from the border with Ukraine.

On 10 March 1944, units of the Home Army (Armia Krajowa) and Peasant Battalions (Bataliony Chłopskie), two major Polish underground resistance movements that emerged during the Nazi-German occupation, attacked Łasków, which had a predominantly ethnic Ukrainian population.

Estimates suggest that around 300 civilians were killed. Among them was a local Orthodox priest, Lev Korobchuk.

On the same day, members of the Home Army also attacked the nearby village of Sahryń, where they are estimated to have killed hundreds more Ukrainians. Ukraine has also submitted an application to carry out exploratory work there.

Poland has granted permission for Ukraine to conduct a search for the remains of Ukrainian civilians killed by Polish resistance fighters during WWII https://t.co/4JeAAhYJcY

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 2, 2026

Work began in Łasków on 6 October and, on Wednesday this week, the UINR announced that it had “discovered the remains of 30 victims…[who] died as a result of the attack of the units of the Home Army and the Peasant Battalion in March 1944″.

Svyatoslav Sheremeta, the head of the Lviv-based Dolya memorial and search centre, which carried out the work on behalf of the UINR, said that they now hope to “conduct exhumation, rebury the dead, and honour their memory with dignity”.

“Thank you to the Polish side for the opportunity to conduct research,” added Alfyorov. “Our common task is to ensure a worthy commemoration of all victims, regardless of their origin and nationality.”

“True reconciliation begins with respect for everyone’s memory, recognition of the pain of the other side, and the common desire for understanding,” said the head of UNIP, which shared images from the search site in Łasków’s Orthodox cemetery.

 

At the time of writing, Polish officials had not yet commented on the development. However, when search work began last week, Rafał Kościański, a spokesman for Poland’s Institute of National Remembrance (IPN), told Radio Lublin that IPN staff were participating as observers.

Wiesław Koman, from the Provincial Office for the Protection of Monuments, added that cooperation between Polish and Ukrainian archaeologists at the site had been “impeccable”.

Meanwhile, Ukraine’s ambassador to Poland, Vasyl Bodnar, told the broadcaster that the work in Łasków was “a step towards reconciliation between our nations”.

“This is happening on both sides of the border and demonstrates the openness of both sides to commemorating the victims of the past conflict,” said Bodnar. “There are differing voices from different sides of the political arena, but this is the right path, one we should have been on for a long time.”

Polish and Ukrainian researchers have exhumed the remains of 115 Polish soldiers who died in 1939 defending Lviv – now in Ukraine but then part of Poland and known as Lwów – during the invasions by Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union at the start of WWII https://t.co/yQNeq2D54E

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 2, 2026

The legacy of wartime massacres has long overshadowed relations between Poland and Ukraine, who have otherwise become close allies since Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022.

In 2017, Ukraine imposed a ban on searches on its territory for Polish victims of the Volhynia massacres, in which Ukrainian nationalists massacred around 100,000 ethnic Poles, mostly women and children.

Poland has recognised those massacres as a genocide. Ukraine rejects the use of that term, and also points to anti-Ukrainian repression in the interwar Polish state and the massacres of Ukrainian civilians carried out by Polish partisans during the war.

In a diplomatic breakthrough last year, Kyiv agreed to lift its moratorium on exhumations. Since then, it has granted permission for Poland to conduct searches and exhumations at a number of locations.

The remains of 55 Poles massacred by Ukrainian nationalists in WWII have been reburied at a ceremony in Ukraine attended by political and religious figures from both countries.

The victims, around half of them children, were exhumed this summer https://t.co/4q3giZhBAL

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 31, 2026

However, tensions over historical issues reemerged this year, when President Volodymyr Zelensky approved the naming of a military unit after the “heroes of the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA)”, the group that led the Volhynia massacres.

That prompted his Polish counterpart, Karol Nawrocki, to strip Zelensky of Poland’s highest honour, the Order of the White Eagle.

However, the two sides subsequently made efforts to reach a diplomatic solution, including a pledge by Zelensky to “grant a substantial number of permits for search and exhumation work”

Poland’s energy ministry has signed an agreement with two state-owned companies, Polskie Elektrownie Jądrowe (PEJ) and Polska Grupa Energetyczna (PGE), setting out responsibilities for preparing for the construction of Poland’s planned second nuclear power plant.

“This is an investment in our security, sovereignty and economic development,” declared energy minister Miłosz Motyka. “Having our own stable energy sources strengthens Poland’s resilience to crises and reduces dependence on external suppliers.”

❗️ @ME_GOV_PL, @PEJ_PL i @Grupa_PGE podpisały dziś porozumienie określające zasady współpracy przy przygotowaniu budowy drugiej polskiej elektrowni jądrowej 🇵🇱

Polska jest 20. gospodarką świata, ale nasze ambicje sięgają wyżej. Nie będzie silnej, niezależnej gospodarki bez… pic.twitter.com/eQ7zWFEolh

— Miłosz Motyka (@motykamilosz) October 13, 2026

Under the agreement, PEJ, which is also responsible for developing a first nuclear project that is already underway on Poland’s northern Baltic Sea coast, will act as the investor and coordinate the project.

PGE, the country’s largest power producer, will prepare preliminary feasibility studies and analyse potential locations for the plant.

However, a decision on selecting an international partner for the project is not expected to be made until next year. The potential candidates include US company Westinghouse, which is involved in the first nuclear power plant, France’s EDF, and Canada’s AtkinsRéalis.

 

The second plant was initially envisaged as a joint project with Korea Hydro & Nuclear Power (KHNP), a South Korean company, under a letter of intent signed in 2022 under Poland’s former government. However, the partnership was never formalised and fell through last year.

Once the new partner has been selected, it will work with PGE to analyse potential sites. The current preferred locations are Bełchatów – home to the largest coal-fired power station in Europe, owned by PGE – and Konin, both in central Poland, because of their existing energy infrastructure and experience in electricity generation.

According to the Polish government’s nuclear strategy – which was last month updated for the first time since 2020 – construction of the second plant is scheduled to begin in 2032, with its first reactor potentially entering service in 2040. That would be one year behind the previously planned schedule.

The government has updated Poland's nuclear strategy for the first time in six years, with the new plan confirming that the first nuclear plant will launch three years later than previously planned, in 2036, and the second in 2040, one year behind schedule https://t.co/vgtuSXLDjZ

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 3, 2026

Meanwhile, Poland plans to begin construction of its first nuclear power station in 2028, with the plant beginning operation in 2036, three years later than previously planned. Together, the two plants are expected to have a combined capacity of up to 9 gigawatts.

The move is part of Poland’s transition away from coal – which still generates around half of electricity, by far the highest proportion in the European Union – and towards cleaner sources of energy, particularly nuclear and renewables.

Under a national energy and climate plan approved in June, Poland aims by 2040 for coal to account for only 0-5% of the energy mix. Around 15-16% will come from nuclear, 7-8% from gas, with most of the rest from renewables: onshore wind (22-27%), offshore wind (18-21%) and solar (14-18%).
