By Daniel Tilles

Poland will hold parliamentary elections a year from now. The outcome will decide who governs the country for the next four years – although, given how close the polls are, and with questions over coalition formation, it could also result in uncertainty, chaos, and even new elections being called.

Below, we explain how the elections work, which parties will be standing, what kind of outcomes are possible, and which issues may animate the campaign.

When will the election take place?

Assuming early elections are not called, the vote must take place on a non-working day in the last 30 days before the end of the current four-year parliamentary term, which began on 13 November 2023.

Because elections in Poland are held on Sundays, that gives four possible dates: 17, 24 or 31 October, or 7 November (though 1 November and 11 November, which are public holidays, are also theoretically possible).

It is the president, Karol Nawrocki, who will choose the date. He must do so no later than 90 days before the end of the current parliamentary term.

How does voting work?

The 460 members of the more powerful lower house, the Sejm, are elected through proportional representation, meaning that seats are distributed more or less on the basis of the share of the vote parties receive (using the so-called D’Hondt method for allocating seats from electoral lists put forward by each party). However, parties must receive at least 5% of the vote nationally to enter parliament (a figure that rises to 8% for coalitions of parties who stand on a single electoral list).

The 100 members of the upper-house Senate are chosen through a first-past-the-post system similar to how members of the US Congress or British House of Commons are elected, with the candidate in each district that receives the most votes winning the seat.

How is a government formed?

A government can only be formed if it has the support of a majority in the Sejm.

After the elections, the president designates a prime minister, who is tasked with forming a government – which would almost certainly be made up of a coalition of parties – that must then win a vote of confidence in the Sejm.

If they fail to do so (as happened in 2023), the Sejm votes to choose an alternative prime minister, who likewise must try to form a government that has the confidence of the Sejm.

Parliament has chosen @donaldtusk as Poland's new prime minister.

That paves the way for him to form a new government in the coming days, ending the eight-year rule of the national-conservative PiS party https://t.co/iZUKh2rxnP

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 11, 2023

If that fails, the president has a second chance to pick a prime minister, who must again win a confidence vote. If that does not work, then parliament is dissolved and new elections are called.

Who is likely to form the next government?

At the moment, it is incredibly difficult to say. Polls suggest an even split in support between parties generally aligned with Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s ruling coalition – which ranges from left to centre right – and the right-wing opposition. However, the 5% electoral threshold complicates the picture.

According to current polling averages compiled by Polish website eWybory and Politico Europe, Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO) leads with 32%. One of its coalition partners, The Left (Lewica), is on 7%, while two others, the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL) and centrist Poland 2050 (Polska 2050), are on around 3% and 1%, respectively. Another left-wing party, Together (Razem), which previously caucused with the ruling coalition but split in 2024, is on around 4%.

Meanwhile, the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), the largest opposition party, is on 20%. Two far-right opposition groups, Confederation (Konfederacja) and Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP), have 14% and 9%, respectively. The right-wing Development Plus (Rozwój Plus), which broke away from PiS this year, is at around 5%.

Rolling 30-day average support in polls for Poland’s main political parties (source: eWybory.eu)

If we treat those as two potential blocs, parties more or less aligned with the current government are on around 47% while the right-wing opposition is on 48%. However, PSL and Poland 2050 currently look likely to fall below the 5% threshold if they stand alone, meaning votes for them would not count. That would significantly harm Tusk’s chances of forming a new government. If Rozwój Plus stood alone and fell below the threshold, that would harm the opposition.

It is therefore likely that, as the elections draw nearer, parties that seem likely to fall below 5% will seek to join forces with other groups. In 2023, PSL and Poland 2050 stood together in the so-called Third Way (Trzecia Droga) alliance. But they have made clear they do not intend to do that again. That leaves them with limited options. They could join forces with KO on a single electoral list, but that does not guarantee that their voters will follow them. Indeed, some may baulk at voting for Tusk’s party.

The Polish People's Party's parliamentary survival is on a knife edge, and could determine whether @donaldtusk's coalition remains in power after next year's elections.@AleksSzczerbiak looks at the challenges facing PSL and how it may respond to them https://t.co/MmswSLNWJE

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 30, 2026

Meanwhile, there are some wildcards in the pack. KKP, led by radical-right extremist Grzegorz Braun, is shunned by the mainstream right for its antisemitism, anti-Americanism and sympathy towards Russia. PiS’s leader, Jarosław Kaczyński, has declared that he would not allow Braun to join government. Development Plus has taken a similar position. Both parties value relations with the US and the Trump administration, whose ambassador to Poland has reportedly pushed them to rule out working with Braun.

However, if KKP maintains its current level of support, it looks almost impossible for the opposition to form a parliamentary majority without it, meaning there would be a strong temptation to somehow work with Braun. Kaczyński’s determination to remove Tusk from power may outweigh his dislike of Braun and desire to keep the Americans onside.

The Together party – if it manages to pass the 5% threshold – could likewise represent a challenge for Tusk when forming a coalition, given that it has criticised the government for failing to keep promises on healthcare spending, public sector pay, and liberalising the abortion law.

 

There also remains the possibility of some elements from each camp joining the other side – either entire parties or individual MPs defecting – in order to help form a government.

PiS has long sought to tempt PSL to its side (and recent reports suggest that even President Donald Trump tried to persuade PSL’s leader, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, to do so). It is conceivable that Rozwój Plus could work with parts of the current ruling camp, though its hatred of Tusk would make that very difficult.

All of the difficulties outlined above mean there is a significant chance that it will not be possible for anyone to form a government, necessitating fresh elections – something that has never happened before in Poland. If that happens, it would mean uncertainty and a lack of clear leadership at a time when Poland is facing major security challenges and a worsening fiscal situation.

What about the Senate?

The Senate, like the Sejm, is currently controlled by the ruling coalition. Indeed, Tusk has an even larger majority there than in the lower house, making it harder for the opposition to flip. Although the Senate is much weaker than the Sejm – and control of it does not determine who forms the government – it does have some powers that make it a useful asset.

It can slow down the passage of legislation, though not block it. The Senate also must approve the appointment of certain officials, such as the heads of the Supreme Audit Office (NIK) and the Institute of National Remembrance (IPN), as well as the Commissioner for Human Rights (RPO).

In a rare clash between Poland’s two houses of parliament, in both of which the government has a majority, the Senate has rejected a candidate chosen by the Sejm to become the new head of the state Institute of National Remembrance (IPN) https://t.co/QUsqfDNh4s

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 7, 2026

The upper house is also required to approve proposals by the president to hold national referendums. This year, the Senate has twice blocked moves by Nawrocki to hold a referendum on EU climate policies.

In a situation where Tusk’s coalition controlled the Sejm, and was therefore still in government, but the right-wing opposition held the Senate, that would give the president a powerful tool to call referendums on policies important to him and the opposition.

To that end, there have been calls for the right-wing and far-right opposition to form a so-called Senate pact, of the type that Tusk and his allies used to win control of the upper house in 2019 and 2023.

What that means in practice is that the parties forming the pact agree to stand only one candidate between them in each of the 100 Senate districts, making it more likely that they will scoop up votes from supporters of all the parties in the pact and win the winner-takes-all contest.

What role will Nawrocki play in all of this?

Presidents are in theory expected to be non-partisan. In practice, however, they will seek to boost parties or coalitions aligned with them, and with whom it will be easier to work.

Since Nawrocki was elected last year, relations and cooperation between the president and government have reached unprecedently low levels. Within just 10 months, Nawrocki had vetoed more bills than any previous president in history over their entire terms. He has made it abundantly clear that he would prefer to work with a government formed from the right-wing opposition.

During his first year, President Nawrocki has transformed his office into a centre of resistance to the government and become a unifying figure for the fragmented right.

But he faces new challenges moving towards the next election, writes @AleksSzczerbiak https://t.co/uNYrFOppSp

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 7, 2026

However, the extent to which he will be involved in the election campaign is unclear. Some figures on the right hope that Nawrocki will act as a figurehead, using his positive relations with parties across the right-wing opposition to bring them together.

In practical terms, this could involve him acting as the patron of a Senate pact (something the head of Nawrocki’s cabinet recently said the president was willing to do), as well as helping right-wing parties form a coalition government after the elections.

Nawrocki also continues to enjoy strong approval ratings among the conservative electorate, meaning that his presence during the election campaign could act as a boost for the opposition.

What issues are likely to feature in the campaign?

A major issue will be the question of sovereignty. The right-wing opposition accuses Tusk of being Brussels’ and Berlin’s lapdog, handing over ever more power to the EU and prioritising Germany’s interests over Poland’s.

The ruling coalition, meanwhile, argues that PiS is too beholden to the Trump administration and warns that the opposition is pushing Poland towards “Polexit” from the EU, which would leave the country isolated and vulnerable, as well as much poorer.

Those battle lines extend to security policy too, with the Tusk government shifting emphasis towards Europe as a defence partner but PiS insisting that only the US can truly guarantee Poland’s security. Poland’s desire to host a new permanent US military base has already become highly politicised. If progress stalls, the opposition will blame the government. If Washington confirms that the base will go ahead, Nawrocki will seek to take the credit, based on his good relationship with Trump.

On this point, though, it is worth noting the split within the opposition. While PiS and Rozwój Plus are strongly pro-American, Confederation and, to an even greater extent, KKP, are opposed to a greater US presence in Poland.

President @NawrockiKn says that a planned new permanent US military base in Poland is “confirmed” because his American counterpart, Donald Trump, is “famous for keeping his word”.

He also suggested that the new facility will be called “Fort Trump” https://t.co/uGGJSBe5nr

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 23, 2026

Where the right-wing opposition has been united, however, is on pushing for a tougher position towards Ukraine and Ukrainian refugees in Poland.

While tensions have calmed significantly since the crisis sparked in May by President Volodymyr Zelensky naming a military unit after a group that massacred Poles in World War Two, it is likely that relations with Ukraine and the large-scale presence of Ukrainians in Poland will remain important issues during the election campaign.

The ruling coalition, meanwhile, will be keen to emphasise its tough overall approach to immigration, which it says was out of control under the former PiS government. It can point to the falling number of new residence permits being issued, the growing number of deportations, and tougher measures on the Belarus border, including a ban on asylum claims.

Poland has forcibly removed 2,100 foreigners from the country this year, around twice as many as in 2024.

The figures come after the government introduced a tougher new migration policy last year, which has included more deportations of foreign criminals https://t.co/zOBxPLipy8

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 31, 2025

The economy, public finances and cost of living are also likely to be major issues.

As long as the current global energy crisis sparked by the conflict around Iran continues, the opposition will seek to place the blame for record fuel prices on the government. They will also cite large deficits and the ballooning public debt as evidence that Tusk is mismanaging the economy.

The ruling coalition will point to continued strong economic growth and blame Nawrocki, who has vetoed revenue-generating tax bills, for the fiscal situation.

In one of his first policy announcements since being elected on Sunday, the new mayor of Kraków, Poland’s second-largest city, has declared that he will withdraw official patronage of its annual LGBT+ equality march.

Łukasz Gibała, who has been supportive of LGBT+ rights in the past and has previously attended the march, argues that the event has become too “partisan”. He stood for election as an independent and has pledged to depoliticise city hall.

His decision does not prevent the march from taking place. But it means that it no longer has the official support of the city.

Kraków’s equality march, which was first held in 2004, draws thousands of participants when it takes place each year in May. The event is used to demand greater LGBT+ rights in Poland, which is ranked as one of the worst countries in Europe for LGBT+ people.

In 2021, the city’s former mayor, Jacek Majchrowski, became an honorary patron of the march. In 2024, his successor, Aleksander Miszalski, became the first mayor to attend the event, declaring that Kraków should be “a home for everyone”.

However, Miszalski was removed from office earlier this year in a recall referendum, necessitating a new election, which was won by Gibała. He beat Monika Piątkowska, who, like Miszaski, is a member of the centrist Civic Coalition (KO) party of Prime Minister Donald Tusk.

Kraków's new mayor has announced that he will attend the city’s LGBT parade next week, something his long-serving predecessor never did.

"I want to build a tolerant Kraków, a home for everyone," says @OlekMiszalski, who took office this week https://t.co/ZQ9SzZiHp4

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 9, 2024

The day after his victory, Gibała was asked by local broadcaster Radio Kraków if he would continue city hall’s patronage of the equality march. The new mayor, who takes office next week, declared that he would not, saying he “will avoid sponsoring events that have a partisan character”.

“I have the impression that, over the past three years or so, the community that organises equality marches has simply become partisan,” said Gibała. “These are people who ran for parliament and local government on the lists of specific political parties.”

Gibała did not indicate who he was referring to. However, one of the organisers of the equality march in Kraków is Magdalena Dropek, who has three times stood as a candidate for The Left (Lewica), one of the groups in Tusk’s ruling coalition, in elections to the Polish and European parliaments.

 

Gibała emphasised that he has himself attended equality marches in the past “and does not regret it”. He was previously an MP for both KO (when it was known as Civic Platform, PO) as well as for the liberal Palikot’s Movement (Ruch Palikota), later known as Your Movement (Twój Ruch).

During the recent mayoral election campaign, Gibała told broadcaster TVN that, as an MP, he had supported the introduction of same-sex civil partnerships in Poland, and said that his views had not changed.

When asked if that meant that, as mayor, he would continue the city’s practice of transcribing foreign same-sex marriages into the civil registry – as Poland was ordered to do last year by the Court of Justice of the European Union – Gibała said that he would.

However, he added that he was doing this as a “legalist” who respects the current legal situation. “If a different political party wins [parliamentary elections] next year and changes the law in Poland, it [recognition of foreign same-sex marriages] won’t happen,” he told Radio Kraków.

In fact, although the current government supports recognition of foreign-same sex marraiges, it has not changed the law in that regard. Polish law still does not recognise any form of same-sex union.

The government, aware that opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki would veto any change to the law, instead issued a regulation (which does not require presidential approval) empowering local authorities to transcribe foreign same-sex marriages into their registries.

Many municipalities, especially more liberal larger cities, have begun to do so (some even did before the regulation was issued). But others, especially in more conservative places, have refused to, often arguing that there are legal doubts around the issue.

Data provided to the Polish Press Agency (PAP) by the digital affairs ministry last week showed that 516 foreign same-sex marriages have so far been registered in Poland. The largest numbers were in Warsaw (209), Wrocław (73) and Kraków (46).

The standoff between the government and opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki over Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) deepened today, as Maciej Berek, whom Prime Minister Donald Tusk recently described as his “right-hand man”, took his oath as a new judge without the presence of the president.

Berek is now the fifth judge to take their oath without presidential approval. The previous four have been denied entry to the TK, and speculation is rife that the government may soon take action to ensure that the excluded judges are able to take up their positions.

PILNE 🚨 dr Maciej Berek złożył w Sejmie ślubowanie na sędziego Trybunału Konstytucyjnego! pic.twitter.com/sZlzLnsL3M

— Bogdan Zdrojewski (@BZdrojewski) October 14, 2026

Under Polish law, a new TK judge must swear an oath “before the president”. However, since Berek was elected to the TK by the government’s majority in parliament in early September, Nawrocki has refused to swear him in.

The president claims that Berek has not presented evidence that he meets the statutory requirement of having practiced as a legal counsel for at least 10 years. Berek says he has done so.

Nawrocki has also expressed his opposition to the fact that Berek has gone from serving in Tusk’s cabinet, where he was minister in charge of overseeing the implementation of policy, to becoming a TK judge.

Even some members of Tusk’s ruling coalition opposed Berek’s candidacy, saying that it contradicted the government’s earlier pledges to “depoliticise” the judicial system, including by banning anyone who had served as a politician in the last four years from becoming a TK judge.

 

With no invitation from Nawrocki forthcoming, on Wednesday morning Berek instead swore his oath at a ceremony organised in parliament. He declared that he was directing the oath towards the president, despite Nawrocki not being present.

The development came a day after the Venice Commission, an advisory body to the Council of Europe on constitutional law, had issued an opinion effectively supporting the government’s position on the crisis around the TK.

The commission found that the Polish president should swear in TK judges chosen by parliament “without delay” and does not have the power to review their election. It added that, if the president refuses to receive a judge’s oath, they are justified in taking it without him being present.

The opinion was welcomed by Tusk and his government. However, Nawrocki’s spokesman, Rafał Leśkiewicz, pointed out that the Venice Commission’s opinions are advisory and not legally binding.

The two leaders signed a declaration on strategic partnership during a visit by a Norwegian delegation to the Warsaw Security Forum, where Norway is this year’s partner country. The agreement sets out a framework for closer long-term cooperation between the two countries.

Among the commitments made by the two countries are “deeper operational cooperation” and expanding joint procurement and production between their respective defence industries.

Warsaw and Oslo also pledged to work together on strengthening NATO’s eastern and northern flanks, as well as to coordinate responses to cyberattacks, hybrid operations and foreign information manipulation.

“The point is that Europe should take on greater responsibility for security,” said Støre. “We must invest in it more coherently and consistently, so as to avoid duplication, but invest in such a way that regional defence systems are stronger.”

 

The declaration also promises continued support for Ukraine in its defence against Russia, as well as efforts to ensure a just and lasting peace and to “hold Russia accountable for its war of aggression”.

Although security issues dominate the declaration, the two countries also pledged to deepen economic ties, including in the energy and maritime sectors.

Robin Allers, a scholar at the Norwegian Institute for Defence Studies, told the Polish Press Agency (PAP) that the move to sign the declaration with Poland was part of a broader Norwegian strategy to deepen mutual commitments with key NATO partners amid uncertainty over US engagement in Europe.

“Today’s agreement demonstrates your country’s increasingly important role in Europe,” said Allers, pointing to Poland’s growing economic and military strength, as well as its role in supporting Ukraine.

Those included a fire that burned down Warsaw’s largest shopping centre, Marywilska 44; another at a store in Warsaw belonging to home improvement chain OBI; and a third at an IKEA store in Vilnius. They also allegedly planned an arson attack on an IKEA store in the Latvian capital of Riga.

Data harvested from mobile phones by the Polish authorities using Pegasus spyware were transmitted outside Poland and were accessible to the tool’s Israeli producer, Polish prosecutors have revealed as part of an investigation into the use of Pegasus under the former government.

Prime Minister Donald Tusk says that the case is “one of the biggest scandals in Polish history since the fall of communism”, and that it is “beyond any doubt” that the Israeli firm behind Pegasus, NSO Group, cooperates with Israeli intelligence.

Tego o Pegasusie jeszcze nie słyszeliście. pic.twitter.com/etvhTE9EWa

— Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) October 12, 2026

Pegasus is a powerful and controversial tool that allows the extraction of large amounts of data from mobile phones without users’ knowledge. A number of countries have been found to have used it to spy on opposition figures.

In 2017, Poland, under the government of the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) party, purchased Pegasus from NSO. The spyware was subsequently used against hundreds of targets, including a number of PiS’s political opponents.

Among them was the head of the 2019 election campaign of Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO) party (which was then known as Civic Platform, PO). Last year, Tusk revealed that his own wife and daughter had been among those caught up in the surveillance.

PiS, however, has insisted that Pegasus was a necessary tool to fight crime and ensure national security. It says the spyware was only used with court approval against targets legitimately suspected of wrongdoing.

 

After a coalition led by Tusk took power from PiS in December 2023, it launched investigations into the use of Pegasus under the former government.

Today, the National Prosecutor’s Office released its latest findings, based on analysis by experts at the forensic research office of Poland’s Internal Security Agency (ABW).

The experts confirmed that Pegasus allowed the harvesting of emails, instant messaging and text messages; the content of telephone conversations, both via mobile networks and internet calls; browsing histories, calendars and contact lists; photos, videos and other files; and location data.

“Additionally, Pegasus allowed the use of the device’s built-in microphone and cameras to record audio and video in real time and take screenshots,” reports the National Prosecutor’s Office.

Czy to możliwe, że państwo traci kontrolę nad własnym systemem inwigilacji? I to nie była stara konsola…

Z opinii biegłych ABW wynika, że CBA kupiło narzędzie, nad którym nie miało pełnej kontroli. Dane opuszczały Polskę, moduł infekujący kontrolował producent, a zagraniczna…

— Waldemar Żurek (@w_zurek) October 12, 2026

The ABW experts also highlighted serious concerns over management and security of the harvested data, noting that Poland’s Central Anti-Corruption Bureau (CBA), which was responsible for using the spyware, “did not have full control over the Pegasus system”.

“The CBA did not have passwords to access some accounts with administrative privileges and some system components remained under the control of the manufacturer [NSO],” wrote the prosecutor’s office. “The server module responsible for infecting mobile devices remained under the manufacturer’s exclusive control.”

Data transmitted through the Pegasus system travelled outside Polish territory, through “servers located in various parts of the world”, in a network managed by NSO and “beyond the CBA’s control”, found the experts.

Meanwhile, NSO “had technical access to materials from operational surveillance”, although prosecutors say that the experts “did not determine whether the manufacturer actually obtained access to materials from specific operations”.

City AM https://www.cityam.com/ London's Business Newspaper Thu, 15 Oct 2026 16:48:32 +0000 en-GB hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.0.7 https://www.cityam.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/app_launcher_icon_final_rounded.png?w=32 City AM https://www.cityam.com/ 32 32 213406410 IMF boss warns on AI ‘tax erosion’ if jobs are wiped out https://www.cityam.com/imf-boss-warns-on-ai-tax-erosion-if-jobs-are-wiped-out/ Thu, 15 Oct 2026 22:00:00 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2466111

The head of the International Monetary Fund has warned financial ministers that widespread AI adoption could erode tax bases across the world as incomes are squeezed by the technology. Kristalina Georgieva, the managing director of the IMF, said governments may be ill-prepared for a potential slump in tax revenue brought on by AI’s impact on [...]]]>

The head of the International Monetary Fund has warned financial ministers that widespread AI adoption could erode tax bases across the world as incomes are squeezed by the technology.

Kristalina Georgieva, the managing director of the IMF, said governments may be ill-prepared for a potential slump in tax revenue brought on by AI’s impact on the labour market. 

At the fund’s summit in Bangkok, Georgieva has issued a series of warnings on the impact of AI, calling the technology a “slow-moving tsunami” that could affect 60 per cent of jobs in wealthy countries. 

In a blog post on Thursday, Georgieva suggested governments would need to “make hard choices” and implement vast tax reform to shift revenue streams from labour to other areas such as land or investment. 

“AI may raise growth, but it could also reduce labour income, increase inequality, and erode the tax base,” Georgieva said. “Countries will need fiscal space to invest in infrastructure and skills, and cushion the impact on the most vulnerable. And they will need tax systems designed for the AI era. 

“With debt already high, policymakers will need to make hard choices.”

AI’s toll on the tax system

In the UK, income taxes account for more than a quarter of total tax receipts. National Insurance paid by workers and employers is another large revenue-raiser, accounting for about 16 per cent of total receipts in 2025-26. 

Revenue is also largely made from levies on the highest earners as the top one per cent pay about 28.5 per cent of all tax. 

Former Chancellor Rachel Reeves announced the launch of the UK’s AI Economics Institute, which is being led by Nobel prize winner Professor Simon Johnson, in order to evaluate and manage the effects that the technology could have on fiscal policy. 

Oxford professor Ben Ansell weighed in on the debate by proposing an “AI token tax”, which would be a levy on the use of models. The Austrian-American economist Anton Korinek, who sits on Anthropic’s economic advisory council, has said that governments should transition from income taxation to consumption taxation. 

In her warning on AI, Georgieva also said that there could be a fall in stock prices that “cascades through the highly leveraged and circular AI ecosystem”, with losses “spread around the world”. 

Her statements echo those of Financial Stability Board chair Andrew Bailey and Bank of England deputy governor Sarah Breeden, who predicted there would be a “correction” in market pricing if company profits disappoint following years of heavy capital investment in AI.

Risks to AI firms and governments come at a tumultuous time for the global economy given ongoing conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East and low growth in Western economies. 

The IMF urged European countries to avoid imposing more protectionist measures, after its ‘Made in Europe’ scheme – designed to boost domestic manufacturers over imports from China – has come under the spotlight. 

Economists advised European leaders to dismiss “rising calls for more interventionist industrial policy” as they would not “durably address Europe’s underlying growth problem”. 

Given large deficits in various major economies across the continent, ministers were also urged to only provide energy support packages that were “tightly targeted at supporting the most vulnerable”.

]]> 2466111Maurício Alencar Maurício Alencar Robert Jenrick hits out at Deloitte and KPMG over job cuts https://www.cityam.com/robert-jenrick-hits-out-at-deloitte-and-kpmg-over-job-cuts/ Thu, 15 Oct 2026 16:01:01 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2466162

Reform UK’s Robert Jenrick has criticised Big Four giants Deloitte and KPMG for laying off British staff, alleging they did so while “importing thousands of migrant workers”. In his latest video post, standing outside Deloitte’s London HQ, the MP said Deloitte “laid off 800 UK staff” but that “over the last five years, they have [...]]]>

Reform UK’s Robert Jenrick has criticised Big Four giants Deloitte and KPMG for laying off British staff, alleging they did so while “importing thousands of migrant workers”.

In his latest video post, standing outside Deloitte’s London HQ, the MP said Deloitte “laid off 800 UK staff” but that “over the last five years, they have hired 8,800 foreign workers.”

Reform’s economic spokesman said Deloitte “are not alone” and alleged KPMG sponsored 1,100 visas and laid off 900 UK staff.

In March, KPMG revealed it was laying off more than 400 staff in its audit department and 120 in its advisory section, citing low attrition rates. In July, City AM revealed KPMG was cutting around 200 staff in its UK group corporate services division. Last month, the FT announced KPMG would lay off another 200 staff in its data and tech division.

Like other Big Four firms, Deloitte has also made thousands of redundancies in the UK over the last few years due to a mix of the fallout from overhiring during the pandemic, an economic slowdown, AI uncertainty, and attrition issues.

This year alone, Deloitte offered voluntary redundancy packages to cut 200 jobs across its audit business, offering UK staff “bumper redundancy packages” that went beyond statutory legal minimums.

Despite Jenrick’s attack that the layoffs are targeting ‘British workers’, the redundancy rounds can also include staff on visas, such as the Skilled Worker visa. Firms don’t publicly disclose the specific visa statuses or nationalities of the individuals included in their redundancy figures.

According to UK Home Office data for 2025, Deloitte sponsored 1,647 workers on Skilled Worker visas, and KPMG sponsored 1,132 workers. Data on the immigration status of people who are made redundant is unavailable.

Reform UK officials told City AM they didn’t have specific problems with KPMG and Deloitte, and instead wanted to see large employers take on more Britons and highly skilled workers.

Reform UK threatened Vodafone boss

Senior figures in the party have clashed with firms of all sizes over migration issues.

Reform UK’s home affairs spokesman, Zia Yusuf, pledged to pay financial rewards to members of the public who inform the government about high street shops employing illegal migrants, after it found several small firms were on a register to sponsor visas even after receiving penalties for employing illegal workers.

Yusuf also threatened to imprison Vodafone boss Margherita Della Valle for supplying free SIM cards to migrants entering the UK on small boats.

Reform has recently taken steps to boost its relationships with businesses, holding its first ‘Business Day’ at the party conference in early September. Jenrick has said party leaders wanted to have an open conversation with bosses about best practices, yet several business representatives have privately criticised the party’s combative approach to building ties with the private sector.

Deloitte and KPMG declined to comment.

]]> 2466162 Maria Ward-Brennan Maria Ward-Brennan Fifa still refusing to share World Cup sell-off papers, says FA chair https://www.cityam.com/fifa-still-refusing-to-share-world-cup-sell-off-papers-says-fa-chair/ Thu, 15 Oct 2026 15:57:28 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2466299

Football Association chair Debbie Hewitt says the Fifa Council is still being denied full transparency over Gianni Infantino’s aborted World Cup sell-off plan. Infantino apologised to the Council today as it met for the first time since controversy erupted over Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE), a new private company Infantino lined up investors for without telling [...]]]>

Football Association chair Debbie Hewitt says the Fifa Council is still being denied full transparency over Gianni Infantino’s aborted World Cup sell-off plan.

Infantino apologised to the Council today as it met for the first time since controversy erupted over Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE), a new private company Infantino lined up investors for without telling the governing body’s supposed steering committee.

But Hewitt said she hadn’t changed her view that Infantino may be criminally culpable, in the absence of documentation she insisted she had repeatedly asked for.

“We didn’t get answers to anything that we had specifically requested, for example getting the papers from FFE,” she said.

“I asked the question ‘why not?’ – and we were asked to submit those questions in writing.

“I think the man has to answer those questions and if he doesn’t answer those questions now, he’s not fit to be Fifa president – and that was what was shared in the meeting.

“I’ve repeatedly asked for the papers to be shared. I haven’t received them and still, in spite of the request today, I haven’t received them.”

Hewitt said she wanted transparency over Infantino’s role in FFE, the Folarin Balogun red card furore at this summer’s World Cup and the awarding of the Fifa Peace Prize to Donald Trump. 

“The responses to those questions, which I still don’t have answers to, will determine from my personal point of view whether or not Gianni is the right candidate,” she added.

“That will be the point at which we can say that any individual that was involved in FFE can or cannot be trusted. Because until we see what actually happened it’s very difficult to say behaviour needs or not to change.”

If you regret it then share it with us, Hewitt tells Infantino

Infantino has resisted calls from top officials in Europe, North America and Asia to step down over the FFE affair and intends to stand, currently unopposed, for re-election in March.

Fifa has also resisted Uefa’s legal attempts to obtain documentation and records of communications relating to FFE in US courts.

Despite Infantino apologising for sidelining the Fifa Council, she said there had been “no holds barred in terms of what we felt about what had happened”.

She added: “If you regret it that deeply, share it with us.

“Those papers coming to Council are a crucial next part of us feeling comfortable as to what, if any, criminal proceedings need to take place.

“From my position, nothing has shifted. I’ve no new information that makes me feel any differently, other than we do have a president who is apologetic.”

Chedid and Salibi rely on Petrofac’s [...]]]>

A group of Lloyd’s syndicates have sought to block £45m in defence funding for two former Petrofac executives facing a criminal bribery trial.

The group of syndicates provided directors’ and officers’ (D&O) insurance coverage to Petrofac’s former chief operating officer, Marwan Chedid, and former chief operations officer George Salibi.

Chedid and Salibi rely on Petrofac’s D&O insurance to cover their legal costs, but the insurers argued the alleged fraud violated the policy. The Lloyd’s underwriters filed a claim in the High Court in August to withdraw the coverage.

In September, Mr Justice Jacobs ruled that the insurers cannot withhold funding and must continue to cover them unless the bribery allegations are proven in court. The parties were at the Court of Appeal on Thursday as several syndicates sought to overturn the ruling.

The costs were covered under a primary and first excess policy, whose limits were nearly exhausted, but the reinsurers provided a second layer of coverage with a £45m limit.

Of the nine insurance firms listed to appeal, only four appealed the ruling, with two being Lloyd’s syndicates Samford Underwriting and Gracechurch UTG (formerly known as ANV). Resinsurance firms MS Amlin and MSI are also appealing. One of the claimants, Liberty Managing Agency, confirmed to City AM that it was not appealing.

SFO trial to commence in November

The Serious Fraud Office (SFO) brought criminal charges against Chedid and Salibi in February 2024 for allegedly offering and paying agents over $30m to influence the awarding of contracts worth about $3.3bn in Petrofac’s favour.

The alleged contracts relate to oil facilities in the UAE, including one for the infrastructure and design of the Gulf’s second-largest oil field, the Upper Zakum Field Development Project.

Both Chedid and Salibi both have pleaded not guilty to the charges. The SFO confirmed to City AM that the trial against Chedid and Salibi, which was due to start on 2 November, will begin on 23 November at Southwark Crown Court.

Petrofac pleaded guilty on 4 October 2021 to seven counts of failing to prevent bribery under the UK Bribery Act.

“This is a very important case for the insurance industry, for white-collar criminal defendants and defence practitioners,” Macfarlanes partner, Lorna Emson, told City AM.

“With the increasing criminalisation of the boardroom, and the widening of scope to attribute the liability of senior management to corporates, the Court of Appeal’s decision in this case will be significant,” Emson said.

Jason Williams, head of division at the SFO, said in a statement: “The SFO is aware of the hearing but is not a party to these proceedings.”

“We continue with trial preparation ahead of our case starting in November 2026.”

Liberty Managing Agency declined to comment.

Petrofac, Chedid and Salibi’s legal representatives, and the insurers’ legal representatives were contacted for comment.

]]> 2466122Rosie Harris-Davison Rosie Harris-Davison Why Peppa Pig and the Lionesses is a partnership to bring home the bacon https://www.cityam.com/why-peppa-pig-and-the-lionesses-is-a-partnership-to-bring-home-the-bacon/ Thu, 15 Oct 2026 14:30:00 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2465941

Peppa Pig and the Lionesses isn’t the most obvious pairing. One’s a muddy-puddle-loving pig loved by my kids and toddlers everywhere and the other is England’s women’s national football team, equally loved by my kids after their heroics in 2025.  But when you take a deeper look behind the Football Association and Hasbro deal, it [...]]]>

Peppa Pig and the Lionesses isn’t the most obvious pairing. One’s a muddy-puddle-loving pig loved by my kids and toddlers everywhere and the other is England’s women’s national football team, equally loved by my kids after their heroics in 2025. 

But when you take a deeper look behind the Football Association and Hasbro deal, it starts to make perfect sense and tells us a lot about the power of partnerships. 

The new character, Libby Lioness, will join the Peppa Pig universe ahead of the 2027 Women’s World Cup and is to be voiced by former England international Jill Scott. What’s more, the partnership will extend into YouTube content, toys, clothing and sporting accessories.

It’s a brilliant way to bring the world of football into children’s lives, particularly girls’. It also shows how brands, broadcasters and the whole entertainment industry can play a role in building the next generation of fans. 

Women’s sport in the UK hit a record 397m viewing hours in 2025, according to the Women’s Sport Trust. Deloitte also predicts global revenues in women’s sports will reach at least £2.2bn for the first time in 2026, up 25 per cent in a year. The growth of viewers means more brands are interested in sponsorship opportunities. 

The commercial value is clear, but the biggest lesson for brands right now is not to wait until tournaments start to get in on the action.

Peppa ultras and football fans offered a route into the other

As the FA and Hasbro deal indicates, partnerships between women’s sports and brands should find ways to bring the game into everyday culture long before the first whistle blows. This helps generate momentum in fan audiences, building communities that converge around the sport at every level, without relying on live games to drum up a dedicated base. 

People discover players through social media, follow their lives off-season, and rewatch match highlights on YouTube. This means that, for younger audiences, the relationship with sport can start well before they ever sit down to watch a full game. 

Any brand can put its logo on a shirt or buy an ad slot around a fixture. But Hasbro shows brands that they can help tell the stories, create the content and build the experiences that make people care in the first place and, importantly, bring women’s football into conversations it might not reach otherwise. 

My toddler doesn’t need to understand the offside rule to enjoy a story about a football character. And, since many parents are forced to watch Peppa Pig, combining the two makes football a shared family experience.  

There are other great examples too, like when Google Pixel partnered with the FA to launch Pixel FC at the last Women’s World Cup. A group of women’s football creators and presenters made critical moments in the tournament accessible and opened up opportunities for girls and women in the game. 

The best partnerships happen when two worlds with already strong narratives — in this case, Peppa ultras and football fans — give each a route into the other. 

It’s a reminder that there’s no one way into women’s sport. Sometimes, it starts with a world-class performance. Sometimes it’s a player sharing a glimpse of life behind the scenes. And sometimes it’s a cartoon pig pulling on a football shirt. 

Sam Bird is SVP, Sport & Entertainment at WPP Media.

]]> 2465941Sam Bird Sam Bird Nvidia’s $250m UK AI bet sparks warning over ‘foreign dependence’ https://www.cityam.com/nvidias-250m-uk-ai-bet-sparks-warning-over-foreign-dependence/ Thu, 15 Oct 2026 14:20:11 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2466240

Nvidia’s $250m investment in the UK’s AI safety research risks deepening the country’s dependence on American tech unless ministers ensure researchers retain control over safety standards, analysts have warned. The world’s most valuable company has pledged $50m a year in computing power over five years to support British research into autonomous AI agents, alongside plans [...]]]>

Nvidia’s $250m investment in the UK’s AI safety research risks deepening the country’s dependence on American tech unless ministers ensure researchers retain control over safety standards, analysts have warned.

The world’s most valuable company has pledged $50m a year in computing power over five years to support British research into autonomous AI agents, alongside plans to invest in five UK startups.

But Indranil Bandyopadhyay, principal analyst at Forrester, warned that heavy reliance on Nvidia’s technology could shape how researchers assess the safety of increasingly powerful AI systems.

“Researchers working mainly on one vendor’s tooling may produce benchmarks that reflect that stack”, he told City AM.

“The AI Security Institute and DSIT should insist on open publication and tie the work to the national evaluation agenda so that the UK, and Nvidia less so, sets the terms of what ‘safe agents’ means”.

The pledge comes amid mounting concerns over autonomous AI agents, which can carry out complex tasks without human intervention, following a series of security incidents involving leading AI developers.

Nvidia will provide computing resources through UK-based data centres to support research at Oxford, University College London and Imperial College London. The $250m commitment provides access to computing power rather than cash grants, giving researchers resources that would otherwise be difficult to fund publicly.

Bandyopadhyay said the investment strengthened Britain’s position in AI safety but raised questions about the US chip giant’s influence over the research underpinning future safeguards.

Chris Beauchamp, chief market analyst at IG, described the announcements as a “co-ordinated bet on the UK as a firm AI hub”.

“It helps to build goodwill with governments while also demonstrating a firm commitment to AI safety”, he told City AM.

Nvidia backs British startups

Alongside its research pledge, Nvidia announced plans to take minority stakes in five British startups: Boltz, Foresight, Hiverge, Prima Mente and Riverlane.

The investments follow similar announcements in France, where Nvidia is backing four startups as it expands its European presence.

Bandyopadhyay said the deals would raise the profile of British tech companies and make further fundraising easier, but warned they exposed a persistent weakness in the UK’s investment market.

“Minority strategic stakes still leave these firms depending on foreign capital to scale, which is the long-standing weakness of the UK ecosystem,” he said.

Russ Shaw, founder of Tech London Advocates and Global Tech Advocates, called the commitment a “great vote of confidence” in Britain’s £1.2tn tech sector.

“Crucially, this goes beyond baseline R&D – it drives commercial translation”, he told City AM.

Nvidia also highlighted the growing use of its technology across British businesses and public services.

Oneadvanced is deploying AI to support NHS patient triage, while Fuse Energy is using Nvidia-powered infrastructure to serve more than 450,000 households in the UK.

But Bandyopadhyay warned that deploying AI in critical services shifts greater safety responsibility onto the companies using it. “For NHS triage, buyers and regulators will need evidence of clinical safety and triage accuracy”, he said.

The announcements came as Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang urged British entrepreneurs to adopt a bolder approach to growth, arguing that the country had the talent but was too focused on failure.

Huang also called for continued dialogue between Western and Chinese AI researchers despite growing geopolitical tensions.

The developments come as ministers face mounting pressure to strengthen Britain’s domestic AI capabilities, with technology executives recently calling for more than £20bn of investment in sovereign infrastructure.

]]> 2466240Saskia Koopman Saskia Koopman Culture secretary Lisa Nandy ‘minded to intervene’ in Sky takeover of ITV https://www.cityam.com/culture-secretary-lisa-nandy-minded-to-intervene-in-sky-takeover-of-itv/ Thu, 15 Oct 2026 14:20:09 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2466261

Culture secretary Lisa Nandy is “minded to intervene” in Sky’s proposed £1.6bn takeover of ITV’s media and entertainment arm.

In a statement to MPs, she said: “Having considered the anticipated merger, I am of the view that there are reasonable grounds to believe that it might affect availability of a wide range of high-quality and varied programming on the on-demand platforms that are now widely used by UK audiences.”

ITV, which is listed on the London Stock Exchange, and Sky have until 20 October to respond to reassure Nandy over competition concerns.

The handover to Sky, which is owned by Comcast, the US media conglomerate that owns NBCUniversal, has put investors and state officials on alert over recent months. 

ITV’s share price has fallen by more than 37 per cent over the last five years, continuing to suffer a fall this year. 

A letter on the possible intervention, which was issued by the Department for Culture, Media and Sport, warned on competition rules and the need for free expression in news media, as well as the plurality of broadcasting and on-demand programmes to appeal to a variety of audiences. 

Bosses have pledged to keep ITV News and Sky News separate until 2030. While Sky News has said its core news offer will remain permanently free, the company has begun exploring additional paid products. A new app on issues around defence and the military charges customers £14.99 per month. 

ITV and Sky’s battle to persuade Nandy

A possible intervention would throw a spanner in the works of a huge takeover deal for UK media. The deal does not cover ITV’s production arm, which makes some popular programmes such as Love Island. 

Carolyn McCall, the former Easyjet boss who now leads ITV, emphasised that top British platforms were competing against the likes of Youtube and Netflix. 

An ITV spokesman said the FTSE 250 firm would “look forward to fully cooperating” with the government following its public interest intervention notice letter.

“This is another important milestone in the regulatory review process towards creating a UK player with the scale and resources to better compete with global streaming platforms benefiting viewers, advertisers and the UK creative industries,” the spokesman said.

A Sky spokesman said: “We will carefully consider the Secretary of State’s letter and look forward to engaging constructively as the review progresses.

“We remain confident that bringing Sky and ITV’s Media and Entertainment business together will create a stronger British media business, better able to compete with global streaming platforms, support great British programming and trusted news, and deliver more for audiences.

“We have already made clear commitments to protect ITV’s identity, its free-to-air services and public service broadcasting obligations, and to ensure ITV News and Sky News remain distinct editorial voices.”

]]> 2466261Maurício Alencar Maurício Alencar Healey’s £1bn London office raid would be ‘attack on growth’ https://www.cityam.com/healeys-1bn-london-office-raid-would-be-attack-on-growth/ Thu, 15 Oct 2026 13:59:45 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2466237

John Healey’s potential £1bn raid on London offices would be an “attack on growth” and deal a huge blow to the City, property firms have warned.  The Chancellor is weighing up an increase to business rates for expensive office blocks and skyscrapers which would raise £1bn for the Treasury but disproportionately hit the capital’s business [...]]]>

John Healey’s potential £1bn raid on London offices would be an “attack on growth” and deal a huge blow to the City, property firms have warned. 

The Chancellor is weighing up an increase to business rates for expensive office blocks and skyscrapers which would raise £1bn for the Treasury but disproportionately hit the capital’s business districts, the Telegraph has reported.

The tax raid threat will raise alarm bells for the City, with bank bosses already fearing Healey could launch an assault on their profits.

The policy would result in “less investment, fewer jobs and lower tax revenues for the whole country,” said the boss of the City Property Association, which represents more than 100 major property developers.

The plans being reviewed by the Chancellor would hike business rates for commercial buildings with a value higher than £500,000. 

The Treasury would exclude the high street from the tax hike by exempting larger retail and hospitality premises from the increase in rates. 

The measure would affect some 9,000 properties in London and the South East, according to tax firm Ryan, with Canary Wharf and the Square Mile being heavily affected. 

Vanessa Hale, chief executive of trade body Real Estate UK, said the government cannot “tax its way to delivering good growth in every postcode” – the key pledge set out by Healey and Andy Burnham ahead of this month’s Budget. 

She said: “House builders are already pulling out of the capital and it seems the government doesn’t care if commercial property developers do too. This isn’t a good growth policy – it’s an attack on growth policy and simply masks the failure to get on and fully reform the business rates system properly.”

Office tax would ‘undermine investment’

CPA chair Nikki Dibley said: “Increasing the cost of occupying office space to the very businesses that are the engines of our economy risks weakening the UK’s competitiveness at exactly the moment we should be making it easier, not harder, for them to locate here and grow. 

“The result is likely to be less investment, fewer jobs and lower tax revenues for the whole country,” she said.

The Midday Market report is a new newsletter from City AM, giving you fresh analysis on the biggest stories in the City straight into your inbox every lunchtime. Today, Ali Lyon, assesses whether August’s positive GDP figures are a sign of a revival in the UK economy. Sign up to the City AM News Updates newsletter here.

For much of the past decade and a half, describing the UK economy has been a relatively easy task. ‘Languid’ has often worked. ‘Stuttering’ has been another favourite. And when things have looked especially sullen, ‘moribund’ or ‘anaemic’ have more than sufficed.

But if today’s GDP figures are anything to go by, then cliche-dependent hacks like this one might find themselves having to reach for their thesauruses in search of a new vernacular.

Granted, a 0.1 per cent jump in economic activity in August is hardly cause to crack open the English sparkling wine. But it was, as almost every economist has been at pains to point out this morning, an expectation-defying 0.1 per cent nevertheless.

The headwinds facing the upward nudge were manifold. And the sources of that resilience – improved productivity, early signs of a tech boom, and an uptick in our, yes, ‘moribund’ manufacturing sector – inspire some confidence.

It is worth reflecting on why quite so many macro analysts are in such a celebratory mood. First, many had – quite understandably – expected the Middle East conflict, now stretching into its eighth month, to finally get its talons into business and consumer sentiment.

Despite what Berenberg’s Andrew Wishart catchily frames as a “quadruple whammy” of rising taxes, higher energy prices, higher mortgage rates and a weak labour market, confidence has, in fact, been improving this year (albeit from a strikingly low ebb). And a look at consumer and services spending in today’s figures shows the trend has, again, defied expectations to the upside.

Then there is the fact that August’s figure was going up against a tricky month-on-month comparative period. Boosted by spendthrift World Cup watchers, the UK economy grew by 0.4 per cent in both June and July, leading most economists to pencil in a minor contraction over the sleepier month of August.

All of which means that over a three months, Britain’s once-languid economy has now grown by 0.7 per cent. It has also jumped 2.1 per cent over the past year, in what is our best 12 months since around 2017.

“The UK’s resilience story continues,” Deutsche Bank’s Sanjay Raja said this morning. “It’s hard to overstate how strong the UK performance has been all year.”

The UK economy’s bleak midwinter

And yet, because we can’t have nice things, there is, I’m afraid, a ‘but’. And that ‘but’ relates to what comes after what most think will be a solid end to the year.

Early forecasts suggest that the start of 2027 could look a lot different from much of 2026. The Bank of England is all but nailed on to raise interest rates at its next meeting in November, with another 25 basis-point hike expected in early 2027. That alone will considerably shift households’ breathing space – and with no end of the inflationary Iran war in sight – price pressure remains uncomfortably hot; especially with the economy chugging along as healthily as it is.

Even more ominous is the direction of energy prices, which are due to build up a head of steam at the start of next year. By the Bank of England’s reckoning, households can expect their energy bills to jump by some 20 per cent in January. That, in turn, will help carry inflation to four per cent, double the monetary authority’s two per cent target. All the while, improvement in people’s pay is expected to slow.

“The combination of rising inflation and slowing wage growth is a toxic mix for households’ real income growth,” says RSM UK’s Thomas Pugh.

Then again, people much cleverer than me have been predicting a sharp economic downturn for much of this year – and it hasn’t materialised. But with so many competing headwinds, overwhelming consensus is we can only be so resilient. Journalists’ thesauruses appear safe… for now.

The German discounter is one of a number of retailers who are vying for a break-up of Poundland. Between six and eight retailers have put in bids for some of its stores, the sources said. 

It had been reported that Aldi, Lidl’s rival, was considering putting in a bid but City AM understands it is not in talks with Gordon Brothers.

Lidl’s involvement in Poundland’s sale comes as the discount supermarket plans to open more than 50 stores in the next year. The grocer has been growing its market share as rival UK supermarkets see their presence in the sector stall.

While Lidl and others have only proposed to buy a specific number of Poundland’s sites, other bidders are proposing to buy hundreds of its shops. 

The owner of The Range and Wilko is among the retail heavyweights battling for control of the discount retailer, The Times has reported. Chris Dawson’s CDS Superstores had been weighing a bid for the entirety of Poundland but is now only interested in parts of the business and a limited number of its locations.

Beyond the retailers hoping to snap up extra sites from Poundland’s sale, a number of investment groups have tabled bids for the business. 

Directors parachuted in as sale speeds up

Poundland’s management have expressed preference for a bid tabled by Martin Property Group (MPG), the Irish firm which recently bought National Car Parks (NCP). 

The discount retailer has parachuted in three independent directors to join its board, Sky News first reported. These new members are Andrew Kirkpatrick, Stephen Welch and Dominic Young.

These directors have been added to the board to address concerns among MPG’s rival bidders that its two existing members, Barry Williams and Shaun Wills, have publicly expressed support for one of the proposals. 

The presence of additional experts on Poundland’s board is intended to offer reassurance to bidders that their proposals will be considered fairly.

“The offers include those from buyers for the whole business and also indicative offers for significant viable parts of the business from established retail operators. 

“The Board will now objectively evaluate these options, considering all relevant stakeholders, with a view to minimising uncertainty for the people, suppliers and local communities with an interest in the business and its future.”

Gordon Brothers kicked off its sale of Poundland last month, little more than a year after buying the company for a nominal £1 fee from retail group PepCo. 

Advisors Alvarez & Marsal, who were appointed to run the sale, are weighing up bids from a number of buyers. These include proposals to carve up the business and offers for the entirety of the company.

Poundland and Lidl were contacted for comment. Alvarez & Marsal declined to comment.

The shadow pensions minister has warned Andy Burnham that he will “live to regret” scrapping the triple lock on the state pension to pay for his new National Care Service.

Speaking at the annual Pensions UK conference on Wednesday, Helen Whately argued Burnham has created a new financial challenge through his commitment to drop the triple lock in Labour’s next manifesto.

Under the system, the state pension would increase each year by either inflation or 2.5 per cent depending on which is highest. This removes the possibility of the pensions spiking from volatile wage growth.

Whately has previously claimed the prime minister is “desperate for cash” to pay for the service, and that slashing the state pension will not bring in enough capital.

Analysis published by the Department for Work and Pensions also showed that, in cash terms, the government will save £15bn a year by 2040. When changes in cash values are accounted for due to inflation, the savings will only come to about £11bn. 

She reaffirmed the Conservative’s stance of maintaining the triple lock if they returned to government, but refused to confirm a reversal to Labour’s changes to salary sacrifice and inheritance tax (IHT) on pensions.

From April 2027, pensions will fall into the scope of IHT, while salary sacrifice contributions will be capped at £2,000 per year.

Improve retirement outcomes

Whately instead urged the government to cut regulation and reduce the tax burden on businesses in order to improve pension outcomes and retirement adequacy, leaving people with enough capital to fund private care in later life.

“The best way to be able to afford better pension provision is to have an economy that’s firing on all cylinders and people being paid better and employers having more margin to address all these problems,” she said.

She added that the burden of the cost of living on both employers and workers was a “huge problem” in saving for retirement, as people are forced to allocate capital to short term issues instead, such as rent.

Whately said: “Lessen the tax burden on businesses…lessen the regulatory burden on businesses.

“And government gets out of the way so that it becomes possible to actually make some money in this country.”

Pension speculation

Whately also warned Healey not to introduce tax incentives as a “bargaining chip” to mandate investment in UK assets in the upcoming Autumn Budget.

“Pension tax relief is not a loophole. It is a vital feature of our pension system. It should not become a bargaining chip to secure the investment decisions ministers want,” she said.

Speculation surrounding changes to pension tax relief has spiralled in the run up to Healey’s maiden Budget on 28 October, including fears the government will only allow pension fund tax benefits if Brits invest a certain amount in the domestic stock market.

The pension industry has warned Healey not to allow pension tax speculation to go “unchecked” in the run up to the Budget, after rumours led savers to pull millions from pension pots last year.

UK savers pulled £91bn from their pension pots before last year’s Autumn Budget as they looked to dodge Labour’s tax raid, according to the Financial Conduct Authority.

Standing in the teeny tiny, Netflix-Christmas-film-coded courtyard outside Cloth Cornhill, I feel sad. This opening drills the final nail in the coffin of the former Simpsons Tavern, the capital’s oldest chophouse, which was on this site since 1757.

Everyone’s got a story about whose fault it is that that chophouse closed. Rumours range from the former tenants being massively overdue rental payments before the pandemic, through to it being the greedy landlord’s fault. Either way, the former manager is bitter that in 2022, his run came to an end – he said this in a lengthy LinkedIn post – and rightly so: he was the final custodian of the Simpsons Tavern brand, which had been in place for 250 years.

In the drizzle, my colleague and I spend 45 minutes admiring the expensive, shiny refurbishment. Nursing pints of ale, we discuss the whole sorry situation. Despite my empathy for the old guard, who still retain the rights to the Simpsons Tavern name and plan to open somewhere else in the “spirit” of Simpsons, it makes for tantalising gossip. I’d love to know what went down, but the landlord is uncontactable. It’s impossible not to feel that the fallout is one big shame. RIP Simpsons Tavern, for now, anyway.

But today, we’re talking about Cloth Cornhill. Founders Ben Butterworth, Joe Haynes and Tom Hurst have recreated the old place as if it were 1757 again. The landlords were so scrupulous, they asked to see sample menus before they’d agree to hand over the keys, so this trio must be, at the very least, charismatic. Just don’t say that anything is in homage to the old venue or ‘bringing anything back’ as that gets them in murky legal waters.

Cloth Cornhill: how about a ‘pie course’?

Its gleaming mahogany high-backed benches have been buffered to within an inch of their lives, the pub reorganised so the feng shui is better – that’s a fancy way of saying it’s easier to get to the bar – and to give more emphasis to the building’s features, such as the front bay window. Period wooden floor replaces lino; two part-time workers spent six months polishing 22 faux vintage brass lamps.

On autumn’s first sodden Monday, the place is heaving. If the brief was to recreate a cacophonous Dickensian tavern, consider that met. Only there are also quiet contemporary enhancements, such as sound dampening added to the ceiling so you can actually have a conversation. One lonely photo of a barmaid with two cakes in front of her boobs hangs upstairs as a reminder of the good old days. I’m told some of the waitresses used to show their breasts if they got tipped enough, and many from the Simpson’s Tavern days have returned after the reopening (I can’t promise they were the ones flashing the customers however).

Former patrons have even demanded the old menu back. Is it pastiche? A little bit. How can it not be? But in 10 years, when the old guard have all died, no one will remember Simpsons Tavern anyway, they’ll just say there’s a really cool old school chophouse called Cloth Cornhill. Such is life.

Prepare your gout stool

As for the food, Victorian gentlemen would be preparing their gout stools. The menu features superlative spins on British comfort food. To kick off, devils on horseback (prunes filled with black pudding and wrapped in bacon) were just divine – dense enough to suck like boiled sweets. ‘Sausage on the side’ with mustard is delicious, the meat both course and smooth (a version of this dish was on the former Simpsons menu, although the owners insist it was inspired by a recipe in a book found during the refit).

We are recommended the ‘pie course’, which is the most hedonistic thing I have ever heard. I decide on venison, bacon and prune, with pastry that was nine tenths butter, and it is obviously banging, a reflection of Hurst’s philosophy: locally sourced meat, diligently cooked and married with the odd unusual ingredient.

We drink loads of booze to induce more hunger, plus we’re at Simpsons Tavern – sorry, Cloth Cornhill – and that’s what you do in here. “This place was known for gout production,” says our waiter, which I think was supposed to make us feel better about over-ordering. The sommelier brings over something from the Southern Rhone to follow a funky rose that tasted like overripe strawberries.

Welsh rarebit – for dessert!

From the mains, a stuffed potato dumpling with taleggio, girolles and saffron should surely be banned by the NHS. It is the sort of amped-up, 21st century comfort food that demonstrates how Hurst is future proofing the classics. It is the precursor to an enormous lamb chop, which was indecently tender, and served with anchovy butter. During our interview, the trio said they were proudly “countercultural” in their apathy towards healthy food, although the beetroot salad with hazelnut, goats curd and chicory is worth ordering.

Dessert tries a little too hard to be modern. We had something chocolatey cut into a fancy shape, which was nice, but we really wanted spotted dick and sticky toffee pudding. Perhaps these felt too on the nose but please, boys, give the people what they want. Welsh rarebit – for dessert! – was more like it, doused in balsamic vinegar and served the way it always has been. The dippy, melted cheese popular from Simpsons Tavern, the waiter says, is off-menu but on hold for the old regulars.

The house martini comes with sherry rather than vermouth, which is a nod to Haynes and Butterworth’s wine trading CV. It works, but mostly in ensuring I fall asleep in front of the TV with the light on when I get home. I’d briefly forgotten about feeling sad about Simpsons Tavern, which either makes me a sellout or Cloth Cornhill very good indeed – I’ll let you decide.

The Big Four have collectively secured over £1.5bn in public contracts so far this year despite the UK government’s pledge to cut spending on external consultants to save taxpayers’ money.

An investigation by market intelligence platform Tussell found the government has awarded KPMG, Deloitte, EY and PwC over £1.5bn in contracts so far in 2026, more than the entirety of 2025, which stood at £1.04bn.

The data showed it was the second most successful calendar year for the Big Four since Tussell began recording in 2012, beaten only by contracting during the height of the pandemic in 2020.

Leading the Big Four, Deloitte secured £650m across 108 contracts this year. The bulk of these wins focused on IT services, digital transformation, and data analytics. Home Office IT spending accounted for the majority of this new work, including a standout £200m contract for Home Office Digital’s Data Services and Analytics (DSA) unit.

KPMG and EY won the largest contract, worth £456m, awarded by the Cabinet Office, which covers training for civil servants over the next two years.

In terms of rankings, despite being the smallest compared to its competitors, KPMG took second place, winning over £413m in government contract work. EY was third, with an overall value of £260m booked so far this year. Despite being the largest, PwC often takes a proportionally smaller share of public sector work than its rivals. It ranked fourth with over £211m.

As the consultancy market tightens due to the influx of AI and private-sector pulling back on external spending due to an economic downturn, government work remains resilient for firms.

Tamzen Isacsson, chief executive of the Management Consultancies Association (MCA), told City AM: “Consultants are playing a vital role in helping government improve public services for taxpayers, and their specialist expertise is in demand in areas such as digital transformation, cybersecurity, AI and organisational change.”

Civil service skills gap challenge

The increase in UK government spending comes after Labour pledged in 2024 to slash taxpayer spending on external consultants.

The government unveiled plans for greater procurement control in November 2024, rolling out a framework to save £1.2bn by 2026 by freezing non-essential consultancy hires and targeting a 50 per cent spend reduction in the years to follow.

However, the government’s biggest challenge is the civil service skills shortage, especially during digital transformation.

Emma Carroll, principal consultant at Source Global Research, told City AM: “Often, consultants are brought in to tackle the most complex projects where specific expertise is needed and where there is a lack of internal talent, and there are some prime examples of this at play at the moment, including cybersecurity, technology implementation (including AI), or data readiness work, where the government simply can’t risk falling behind.

“The defence sector has also been a critical area of focus for the UK government this year, and consulting support has been and will continue to be important here,” she added.

Source predicts the UK public sector consulting market will grow by around five per cent in 2026, versus around six per cent for the wider consulting market.

Isacsson added: “We recognise the fiscal pressures facing government and share its ambition to improve productivity and delivery across the public sector. Effective use of consultancy helps government do more with less, bringing in specialist expertise where it is needed, supporting innovation, and building capability inside the civil service for the future.”

The Cabinet Office was contacted for comment.

CV

What was your first job?

On the checkout at Tesco in Milton Keynes. I was pretty quick with the scanner and regularly got asked if I was paid by the beep.

What was your first role in the City?

I started out as a graduate accountant at PwC in audit. I worked with a real mix of businesses, from oil companies to nightclubs. I actually wanted to be a doctor, but some work experience quickly made me realise it wasn’t the career for me. I love the mix of old and new. One minute you’re walking past St Paul’s and all that history, the next you’re looking up at a brand new building.

And any business faux pas?

And who do you look up to?

Bang your fists on the table more to get your own way. I’ve always found there are better ways to bring people with you.

Any pub on Watling Street. There’s always a great atmosphere after work, you can’t really go wrong.

Usually out walking my dog, Maverick, or ferrying my children around. My weekends involve quite a lot of unpaid taxi driving.

Britain risks becoming “second in the queue” for AI unless it invests more in domestic infrastructure, a government AI adviser has warned, as Starling Bank becomes the first lender to train an AI model on a UK sovereign cloud.

Harriet Rees, Starling’s chief information officer and the Treasury’s AI champion for financial services, warned that British banks’ reliance on a handful of US tech giants was exposing the financial system to geopolitical risks.

“We’re always going to be second in the queue if we don’t have our own infrastructure, our own models, and some of this stuff really based here in the UK,” Rees told City AM.

Her warning comes as Starling announced plans to develop an AI model using more than 15bn anonymised transactions, trained on infrastructure owned by British cloud provider Civo, using Nvidia technology.

The bank plans to deploy the model in early 2027, initially to improve fraud detection before integrating it into its AI financial assistant.

Rees, who co-authored the government’s financial services AI adoption plan in July, warned that dependence on American cloud providers such as Amazon, Microsoft and Google could leave banks vulnerable to political disruption.

“If it becomes a political matter, then we have less resilience, and that’s why things like sovereign AI become very much to the fore,” she said.

While banks have safeguards against cloud outages, Rees said foreign ownership posed risks that technical backup systems could not fully address.

Government urged to boost UK AI investment

Rees called on ministers to increase investment in British AI infrastructure, arguing that the government’s £500m Sovereign AI fund fell short.

“Anyone in this space knows that £500m pounds is really not a lot of money”, she said. “If we’re serious about this, we need to be able to dig deep into the pockets.”

Her comments follow calls from British tech bosses, including executives at BT and Leonardo, for more than £20bn of investment in sovereign AI infrastructure over five years.

Rees acknowledged that British cloud providers struggled to compete with the scale and resources of American giants, but rejected suggestions that the UK should accept permanent dependence.

“I think we should absolutely have the ambition to have great AI infrastructure companies based here in the UK,” she said.

She suggested ministers could incentivise businesses to use domestic providers, arguing that British cloud services should be cheaper and easier to access.

AI squeezes job market

The announcement comes three months after Starling revealed plans to cut 130 jobs while increasing investment in AI.

Rees insisted the restructuring was not directly linked to automation, but acknowledged that the technology would reshape banking employment.

“This technology fundamentally will change people’s jobs. It will mean that some things that humans had to do no longer need to be done by a human,” she said.
