So far, Sadiq Khan’s only transport achievements have been to cut the ribbon on new projects that his predecessors started, writes James Ford

In recent weeks there has been a flurry of activity regarding London’s pipeline of proposed new transport infrastructure projects. Transport for London (TfL) is finally running a public consultation on the West London Orbital rail project. A laundry list of transport projects has been touted in the Evening Standard, presumably with TfL’s connivance. And the results of a previous consultation on the DLR extension to Thamesmead have been made public, showing significant popular support. Should we conclude that London is finally getting the infrastructure it needs? Of course not.

Rather than a feeling of excitement about new lines and new stations, the correct response you should have is a profound sense of déjà vu. The four grands projets at the top of TfL’s pipeline – Crossrail 2, the West London Orbital, the DLR extension and the Bakerloo Line extension – have all been on TfL’s to-do list since well before 2016, when this Mayor assumed office. Worse still, the biggest project (Crossrail 2) has been mothballed since November 2020. The earliest that it could open is the 2050s.

The sad truth is that this ‘new’ activity is all stuff that a good Mayor of London would have done in their first year in office, not their tenth. And, if you somehow forgot to start campaigning for all this investment and infrastructure in your first year (or even your first term), then Sadiq Khan had a rare second chance to set the ball rolling in the summer of 2022 when the Elizabeth Line opened. In that moment London swooned with excitement about how this Tube line had delivered beautiful stations, faster journey times and new connections. Londoners flocked to the new line in huge numbers and TfL’s coffers overflowed with extra fares income. That would have been a good time to announce that London’s next big project – whichever one it was – had got the green light.

But no, it seems that City Hall and TfL are only now slowly creaking into gear to deliver the infrastructure that London needed in 2016. This decade of delay means that these projects are all set to cost more to build. In 2016, Crossrail 2 was set to cost £32.6bn. By 2019 costs had spiralled to $41.3bn. Now it is thought to cost an estimated £45bn. Between 2020 and 2026 alone the cost of the DLR extension doubled.

What has Sadiq Khan achieved in transport?

In the decade since 2016, the economic and political situation has deteriorated. The government’s focus is on the north, not London. It has signalled support for the £45bn Northern Powerhouse Rail scheme but has so far refused to commit to chip in towards the £1.7bn cost of the DLR extension. At the same time, TfL’s ability to fund this project from its own funds has declined. TfL was carrying debt of £9.1bn in 2016 but £13.9bn in 2026, making it currently the most indebted local authority body in the UK. The second most indebted local authority in the UK? Well, that’s City Hall of course, with £4.7bn of debt.

So far, Khan’s only transport achievements have been to cut the ribbon on new projects that his predecessors started. The Elizabeth Line was approved under Ken Livingstone in 2007 and broke ground under Boris Johnson in 2009. The Northern Line extension to Battersea was greenlit two years before Khan was elected. And Boris also approved the Overground extension to Barking Riverside a few months before he left office.

I, for one, am glad that these vital infrastructure projects are no longer stuck in limbo. But we do have to reflect on what this lost decade has cost London. This sudden, dramatic burst of activity by City Hall and TfL may seem like progress but it is a sad, desperate race for a meaningful legacy from a mayor that is all too aware he is running out of time.

James Ford was an advisor to former Mayor of London Boris Johnson

Two of Britain’s biggest gambling operators have warned John Healey that further tax increases in this month’s Budget could force betting shops and casinos to close, putting jobs and investment at risk.

Entain, the owner of Ladbrokes and Coral, and Rank Group, which operates Grosvenor Casinos and Mecca Bingo, issued separate warnings on Thursday despite reporting growth in their UK businesses.

Entain said net gaming revenue rose two per cent in the third quarter, with its UK and Ireland business growing eight per cent, driven by a 14 per cent jump in online revenue.

Chief executive Stella David urged the government to reconsider any further tax increases on the sector.

“We strongly urge the UK government to carefully consider any further gambling tax increases which would threaten the viability of many shops, jobs and livelihoods”, she said.

Rank chief executive, Richard Harris, warned that speculation over further gambling tax increases was already weighing on the company’s investment plans and could lead to layoffs.

“Any increase to Machine Games Duty will increase costs, reduce venue viability, lead to venue closures and job losses, reduce tax receipts and halt investment”, he said.

The company reported a five per cent rise in like-for-like net gaming revenue to £216.1m in the three months to September, supported by growth across its casinos and digital operations.

Its Grosvenor venues recorded six per cent growth, while digital revenue also climbed six per cent.

Gambling firms brace for Budget tax rises

The warnings come ahead of Healey’s first Budget on 28 October, where the chancellor is expected to launch a series of tax rises to bolster the public finances amid higher borrowing costs and spending pressures.

Gambling companies have faced growing scrutiny over their tax contributions, with speculation that the Treasury could target the sector for additional revenue.

Rank said its UK digital business had remained resilient despite higher taxes introduced in April, although it had reduced marketing spending.

The company also closed three venues during the quarter, in Swansea, Reading Central and Sunderland, which it said were no longer economically viable.

It maintained its full-year profit expectations, assuming no further changes to the current UK tax regime.

Entain also reiterated its annual guidance, although it expects underlying earnings at the lower end of its £910m to £960m range.

Its international business remained under pressure, with revenue falling four per cent amid difficulties in Brazil, where the government introduced an immediate ban on online gambling in September.

The group’s US joint venture BetMGM provided a brighter spot, reporting third-quarter revenue of $710m and adjusted earnings of $86m, more than double the previous year’s figure.

Entain said it continued to expect online revenue growth of between four and six per cent for the full year.

A London fintech backed by employees of OpenAI and some of the world’s biggest banks has raised $1.6m (£1.2m) to help financial firms navigate mounting regulatory requirements using artificial intelligence.

Relace, founded by a former lawyer and an AI engineer, has secured the pre-seed funding in a round led by Boost Capital, with backing from Ascension, Koro Capital and angel investors from JPMorgan, Barclays, Morgan Stanley, OpenAI and SAP.

The startup has also been selected for the Financial Conduct Authority’s (FCA) Supercharged Sandbox, a programme supported by Anthropic and Nvidia that allows firms to develop and test advanced AI tools for financial services.

Relace was one of 21 companies chosen from 199 applicants for the programme’s second cohort, which runs until the end of 2026.

Its platform uses AI to identify which regulations apply to a financial business, assess whether it is meeting those obligations and flag potential gaps.

The company argues that much of the industry’s compliance work still relies on spreadsheets, lengthy documents and external legal advice, slowing the launch of new products and expansion into overseas markets.

“The challenge is really how regulation is implemented”, co-founder Justin Peimani told City AM.

“If you think about the volume of rules, it has only increased over the last decade, and with AI, cybersecurity, deglobalisation, there’s only more and more rules that are coming”.

Peimani, a New York-qualified lawyer who previously built enterprise software used by major banks, said the shortage of qualified compliance professionals was adding to the pressure.

He argued that technology could help firms make better use of existing staff rather than simply cutting costs.

“The real value comes in risk and in revenue”, he said, adding that one customer had identified 21 previously unknown risks using the platform.

The startup, which has not disclosed its revenue or valuation, said it plans to use its fresh funding to hire engineers, expand its regulatory coverage across the UK, EU, US and Middle East, and build its commercial team.

Relace is already working with Gemcorp Capital, a private credit investor managing around $7bn in assets.

Its chief compliance officer, Patrick Nyamangunda, said work that would typically take weeks had been completed in days across two jurisdictions.

FCA backs AI push into compliance

The funding comes as the FCA faces growing pressure to support innovation and growth in Britain’s financial services industry without weakening consumer protections.

The watchdog has expanded its support for fast-growing firms in recent months, including launching a dedicated Scale-up Unit offering businesses closer access to regulatory officials.

Relace’s work in the Supercharged Sandbox focuses on the FCA’s Consumer Duty rules, which require financial firms to deliver good outcomes for retail customers.

Co-founder Lyubomira Dimitrova, who previously scaled AI infrastructure at identity verification firm Onfido, said access to industry experts had been among the programme’s biggest benefits.

“The mentors have been really good, and the fact that they have managed to create this ecosystem is really important”, she told City AM.

However, the founders acknowledged that convincing financial institutions to trust AI with sensitive regulatory work requires safeguards.

Dimitrova said the platform combines AI with more conventional software methods and provides references for its conclusions, allowing compliance teams to check and amend the results.

“We are not taking away decision-making at any point at all”, she said.

Peimani added that responsibility for meeting regulatory obligations would remain with financial firms, regardless of which technology providers they use.

“The regulator, particularly in this country, is very, very clear that the ultimate responsibility sits with the firm”, he said.

The Independent Football Regulator has improving English clubs’ failing finances in its sights but its treatment of Manchester City is what will likely define it, writes Ed Warner.

What word or phrase to you best describes the state of English football? Would broken, bust or (morally and/or financially) bankrupt fit your bill? A tad sensational, maybe. 

Or you could be a free marketeer to the core, happy to luxuriate in the quality of the players and matches available to a global audience every weekend, regardless of the competing teams’ finances. Perhaps then brilliant or beautiful might describe the game as you personally experience it.

The now-not-quite-so-new Independent Football Regulator has just published the draft of its inaugural State of the Game report. Unsurprisingly short on hyperbole – positioned neither at the broken nor beautiful end of the perception spectrum, it being the work of a regulator, after all – the financial facts the report lays out nevertheless speak for themselves.

The IFR does, though, allow itself one punchy statement in a suitably hefty font: “English football is underpinned by contradictions. It is simultaneously the richest, best and most deeply competitive in the world, but it’s also standing on the edge of a financial disaster.”

Dress these facts up however you wish, any reader of the IFR’s analysis must surely recognise that football in England relies almost entirely on the assumed willingness of new investors being prepared to bolster or bail out current owners of loss-making clubs. The greater fool theory is writ large across 116 men’s professional teams.

Forget their P&Ls; marvel at the intangible asset values instead.

It would be easy to dismiss the economics of this industry as nuts, but you could have been saying the same thing for many years. Yet club valuations continue to inflate, fresh buyers emerging – whether tech bros, private equity titans, luvvies, sport stars or local fans made good in business – to validate the rising values.

On a club by club basis, the music does occasionally stop, and the last buyers of failing enterprises are then exposed as the greatest fools. But there is no sign yet of a bursting of the collective bubble. 

Think any of the many potential investors circling clubs today will be put off by the IFR’s report? Think again. Nor, remember, do clubs often disappear, in spite of their precarious finances. Very rarely, in fact.

How, then, are we to judge the success of the IFR in the years ahead? I’ve written before that I don’t consider it a necessary creation. Partly this is the result of my innate free market tendencies – show me a genuinely effective regulator in any industry, please – but also the belief that football should have the ability to organise and police itself.

The football regulator is here now, though, and so I’m happy to align myself with its proponents to wish the IFR every success in pursuing its remit. Whether we will all be able to agree on its KPIs is another matter.

It is possible that the IFR’s reputation will be forever set in stone according to its handling of the Manchester City case. Footballing and financial penalties will be levied by the Premier League, and possibly in turn by the FA. However, football fans will doubtless look to the regulator to opine on whether Man City’s leaders and owners are fit stewards of the club in the light of the guilty verdicts adhering to it – and by extension them as individuals.

“I’m not going to comment on any actions we might take until we have had a chance to assess it.”

David Kogan, IFR chair

Parallel universes do not exist – or if they do, it’s only Hollywood that can access them – so we’ve no way of knowing whether an IFR would have ruled against the Abu Dhabi United Group’s purchase of Manchester City back in 2008. 

Nor, had the takeover been waived through, whether it would still have required the hacking of emails to unearth the club’s financial misdemeanours; whether the regulator would have got there first instead; or whether its very existence would have proven sufficiently threatening to prevent the rule-breaking in the first place.

Without the opportunity to have proven its chops, the new regulator now has one shot at establishing its governance oversight credentials. As we have seen in the past couple of weeks, the Man City case has political and diplomatic dimensions, meaning any decisions the IFR might make will take on an import far beyond the stewardship of a single football club – albeit the dominant one in the English game for the best part of two decades.

It is probably fair to say that however long the regulator exists for, it will never handle a more significant case. Quite the baptism of fire. 

David Kogan, the IFR’s chair, might secretly wish his organisation had been established a little while after the Man City resolution rather than just before the guilty verdicts. Rest assured that every single decision he and his colleagues make in the years ahead will be viewed through the prism of the conclusions they reach about City.

What of those other KPIs? Root out dodgy owners, save honest but over-enthusiastic ones from folly, play a role in a financial rapprochement between the Premier League and EFL, create greater awareness and understanding of football’s economics among the sport’s fanbase, and encourage greater and better engagement between clubs and their supporters. Some of that will be spreadsheet-jockey work; much of it down to communication and suasion. Easy on paper…

The state of the game? Neither broken nor beautiful. Bonkers sums it up for me. There resides the IFR’s challenge.

Signed in (clean) blood

I was fascinated to read Sean Ingle’s piece in The Guardian this week about the women’s marathon world record, set by Ruth Chepngetich at the 2024 Chicago marathon and still held by the Kenyan in spite of a failed drugs test just five months after the event. A clean test after the race means she can’t be stripped of her mark.

A solution to the sport’s apparent embarrassment isn’t beyond the wit of mankind. Back in the day, at UK Athletics we introduced a new clause to the Team Member Agreement for GB athletes. By signing the agreement they recognised that if they were ever subsequently found guilty of a serious doping offence they accepted that they were no longer eligible to be selected for British teams.

At the time lawyers quaked, citing double jeopardy. But of course, no athlete refused to sign. Why would they? If clean, they would have nothing to fear. To my knowledge, UKA has never had to invoke the clause, although I believe in the intervening years it has been dropped from the TMA (I guess the quaking lawyers won out).

Could this, however, provide a blueprint for World Athletics? Decide a sensible period within which any failed drugs test would invalidate a record (two years perhaps) and then either require athletes to sign up to the new regulation ahead of any eligible competition, or perhaps more simply require a signature from them after a record is set as a condition to it being admitted into track and field’s record book.

There you go, job done (until the lawyers start to quake).

Red, red whine

Day one, first Test between South Africa and Australia. Top two red-ball nations in the world at Durban’s 25,000 capacity Kingsmead stadium. Attendance? Just over 4,000, many of them Aussie tourists.

We get a bigger crowd than that for a T20 Blast match on a Hove Friday evening with none of the ‘sandpapergate’ PR build-up that this Test garnered. Is it any wonder South Africa had played just six Test matches since winning the ICC World Test Championship final in June 2025 – none at home – before the current series?

Or if the Proteas had played more often, might there have been greater local interest. Out of sight, out of mind…

Ed Warner is chair of Sussex Cricket and GB Wheelchair Rugby and writes his sport column at sportinc.substack.com

    Law firms are facing a new challenge as corporate clients are increasingly using their own in-house legal teams and AI tools to do legal work themselves, threatening the traditional growth and revenue model.

    According to new research from HSBC in their yearly UK Law Firm Strategy and Investment Survey, almost three-quarters of 100 law firms the bank surveyed said greater use of technology in legal delivery is driving disruption, while 60 per cent cited clients bringing more work in-house.

    Corporate clients are increasingly bringing work in-house to be managed by internal legal departments, and using AI tools to help, which is leaving firms scratching their heads over how to charge for their highly specialised services which have historically been billed by the hour.

    “Clients increasingly try to do more for themselves, and their accessing plenty of their own AI tools in order to do it,” Pennington Manches Cooper chief executive, Helen Drayton, said.

    “Some clients can also arrive at meetings with their own AI-generated strategies which the lawyer must spend time advising against. How do you decide how to charge for that?” Drayton said.

    As well as this, some clients are side-stepping law firms’ services by using AI tools the firms have suggested themselves.

    David Beech, chief executive of the London-listed law firm, Knights, said many clients’ General Counsels (GCs) “may even be using the likes of AI solutions that partner firms have themselves recommended or developed to meet their needs.”

    “This finds firms more pressured to make the case for an ongoing relationship and regular work where they believe they continue to add most value to a set of problems,” Beech said.

    Victoria Ritchie, head of professional and business services at HSBC told City AM, AI is “already challenging the traditional law firm operating model, accelerating changes in how legal services are delivered, priced and resourced.”

    AI integration ‘a major organisational challenge’

    As well as this, of all the organisational challenges HSBC asked the law firms to comment on, effective AI integration came out as the most frequently cited challenge, with 73 per cent reporting they see integrating AI as a “major organisational challenge.”

    “The legal organisations that succeed will combine innovation with trust, speed with discipline, and technology with human judgement,” Ritchie continued.

    Commenting on the findings, finance director at Roythornes, Sam Elkin, said law firms are “now wrestling with a very different dilemma: what a fresh wave of potentially transformational technology will now mean for the business model of a law firm as pressure builds to see advantages of genAI investment”.

Most people protect their digital lives with a handful of passwords they've memorized—a security practice so common it's become catastrophic.]]>

For about five months, a browser extension sat quietly on the home computers of 154 people and watched them log in.

The researchers never saw a password. Everything was hashed on the machine before it went anywhere, leaving them with the shape of each one: its length, its mix of characters, the site it was typed into, and whether the same string had appeared before.

Very often, it had.

What 154 people actually typed

Sarah Pearman and her co-authors at Carnegie Mellon University presented the results at a 2017 computer security conference, having followed each participant for an average of 147 days. Those people logged in across 26 web domains apiece and covered the lot with fewer than 10 distinct passwords.

Roughly 60 per cent of those distinct passwords were recycled, either typed identically on another site or built around a chunk of four or more characters lifted from one the same person used elsewhere.

Banking got no special treatment. Around 85 per cent of the passwords on financial sites appeared elsewhere too, and nearly all of that crossover ran into unrelated categories, so the login for a savings account was also the login for a shoe shop.

What partial reuse looks like up close

Mostly it looks like adding a character.

Among passwords that shared a substring with another, the most common gap between the two was a single character. Digits were the strongest predictor in the Carnegie Mellon model, multiplying the odds of reuse by more than twelve. The authors’ own explanation is that a password with a number in it satisfies more websites’ fussy signup rules, so it travels further.

The tidy minority had barely any accounts

Ten participants mostly built something new for each site, which sounds like a win for good habits until you look at what they were doing online. With one exception, every one of them entered passwords on eight domains or fewer, and they were active on their computers on only 17 per cent of the days they spent enrolled.

The heavy users went the other way. Ninety-four participants, the largest cluster by far, both copied passwords outright and modified them, and they averaged 32 online accounts each. Discipline held up fine at eight accounts and collapsed at thirty.

The password manager result, with a handbrake

Only 19 of the 154 participants had a password manager installed, and the study found no measurable effect on either reuse or strength.

That result deserves caution. One paper is one paper, the subgroup is tiny, and the software could not tell whether people were generating random strings or merely parking passwords they had invented themselves. Rick Wash and colleagues at Michigan State University, who watched 134 participants over six weeks, found each password being reused on 1.7 to 3.4 websites. Their study did not measure partial reuse at all, so the higher figure out of Pittsburgh partly reflects counting a habit nobody had counted before.

Why a recycled password is worth money

Somewhere there is a text file with an old forum password in it, sitting in a folder alongside a few hundred million others. Troy Hunt, the Australian security researcher behind the breach notification service Have I Been Pwned, has documented the trade in combo lists, which are exactly that: vast dumps of email and password pairs scraped out of past breaches. Cheap automated tools fire them at unrelated websites until one opens. Defending against it is awkward, because a successful run looks identical to a customer logging in correctly.

One shared string, and the breach at a defunct hobby forum becomes a problem at an email provider.

The rules that encouraged this have been withdrawn

In 2025, the US National Institute of Standards and Technology finalised revision 4 of its digital identity guidelines, and the password section reads like a quiet apology. Websites must stop demanding mixtures of character types, and they must stop forcing periodic changes unless there is evidence of compromise. Password managers and autofill have to be allowed, and every new password gets checked against blocklists of strings already known to have leaked.

Each of those requirements targets the behaviour the extension recorded: a handful of memorable strings, nudged sideways by a digit, stretched across an entire online life.

The standard now assumes a machine is doing the remembering. Anyone who ever stuck a “1” on the end to get past a signup form was just covering the shift until it arrived.

]]> A telemarketer refused to keep his webcam on for nine hours a day while working from home and was fired the next day — a Dutch court ruled the demand invaded his privacy and ordered his employer to pay him roughly €75,000 https://siliconcanals.com/d-a-telemarketer-refused-to-keep-his-webcam-on-for-nine-hours-a-day-while-working-from-home-and-was-fired-the-next-day-a-dutch-court-ruled-the-demand-invaded-his-privacy-and-ordered-his-employ/ Tue, 22 Sep 2026 14:15:27 +0000 https://siliconcanals.com/?p=109737

A Dutch court sided with a worker who refused constant video surveillance, forcing his employer to pay damages—a warning shot across the evolving battle over remote work monitoring.]]>

A camera that stayed switched off cost a Florida software company about 75,000 euros.

It belonged to a telemarketer working from the small Dutch town of Diessen, employed since January 2019 by Chetu, an American software firm that at the time ran a Dutch office in Rijswijk. On 23 August 2022 he was told to join something called the Corrective Action Program, which meant staying logged in for his whole shift, sharing his screen and leaving his laptop camera on. He shared the screen. The camera stayed dark.

His objection was brief and entirely unlegalistic. Court filings quoted by The Register record him saying he was not comfortable being monitored for nine hours a day, calling it “an invasion of my privacy” and noting that his laptop activity was already visible to management.

Two more instructions followed, each firmer than the last. On 26 August he was dismissed on the spot, the stated reasons being refusal to work and insubordination.

Three days from the first instruction to the sack.

What the company argued

Chetu’s case, set out in the published judgment of the Court of Zeeland-West-Brabant, was that watching a remote worker through a webcam is no different from a manager walking past a desk. Performance software already sat on the man’s laptop, and that was not considered enough. Chetu wanted to see him working.

Nobody from the company turned up to make the argument in person, as TechCrunch noted, so it went undefended.

What the judge decided

Ruling on 28 September 2022, the subdistrict judge in Tilburg found that ordering an employee to keep a camera running for a full shift conflicted with his right to respect for private life, and that nothing had been offered to justify it. An unreasonable instruction cannot be unreasonably refused, so there had been no refusal to work and no grounds for summary dismissal.

Data protection law dropped out early. On the understanding that no footage would be recorded, stored or used for anything, the judge treated the monitoring as falling outside data processing altogether, and tested it directly against Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights, alongside Strasbourg case law holding that filming staff at work, covert or not, is a serious intrusion into private life. Had the images been kept, the analysis would have looked quite different.

One much-quoted line deserves care. Coverage including a report in Fortune presented the claim that all-day camera tracking is disproportionate and not allowed in the Netherlands as a finding of the court. In the Dutch record it sits among the employee’s own submissions. What the judge actually held was narrower, and sufficient: this instruction, to this man, in his own home, breached Article 8 with no justification advanced.

Why the sum was so large

Almost none of the money was a penalty for the privacy breach. The largest slice, 50,000 euros, was a billijke vergoeding, an equitable award Dutch judges reserve for employers whose conduct in ending a job has been seriously culpable, with a wrongful summary dismissal among the standard triggers, as the Amsterdam employment firm Workx Advocaten explains. Privacy is why the sacking failed. The sacking is what got billed.

Around that sat roughly 8,375 euros for ignoring the notice period, close to 9,500 euros in statutory transition payment, more than 2,700 euros in unpaid wages, 23 days of untaken leave, the 8 per cent holiday allowance and some 585 euros in costs, all itemised by NL Times. His non-compete clause was lifted as well, leaving him free to walk to a competitor.

How common all-day camera rules are

Is this a bizarre one-off or a policy plenty of people are quietly living with? A survey of 1,000 business leaders at mostly remote companies, commissioned by ResumeBuilder in March 2023, found 37 per cent required staff to sit on a live video feed, and that 93 per cent of those firms had somebody monitoring it, usually for four hours or more a day.

The same survey found 73 per cent had dismissed workers on the strength of monitoring data, and 69 per cent had lost staff who would not accept it.

One survey is one survey. It polled American executives, it relied on self-reporting, and executives describing their own management habits are not a neutral instrument. Treat it as a temperature reading rather than a census.

Where the line actually falls

Whatever this settles, it settles in one jurisdiction, on one set of facts, at the lowest rung of the court system. Article 8 offers nothing in Florida, where employment is generally at will and can end without a stated reason, subject to the usual exceptions for discrimination, retaliation and whatever a contract says.

What the case supplies is a price tag on a boundary that remote-work policy has been drifting across without much thought: supervising the work is one thing, keeping a lens open in somebody’s house for the length of a shift is another. A Dutch judge has now looked at that question once, and the employer left lighter.

Agility says Digit 5 is engineered for unfenced work near people; its runtime, charging and daily-productivity figures remain manufacturer specifications ahead of planned 2027 customer access.]]>

Correction, 1 October 2026: An earlier version miscounted the number of charge cycles in a 24-hour day and said early access was more than a year away. The idealised 90-to-9-minute ratio implies about 21.8 hours of runtime and 2.2 hours of charging; early access is planned for the first half of 2027.

Agility Robotics has unveiled Digit 5, the fifth generation of its bipedal warehouse robot, and the headline change is the safety cage — specifically, its absence. Earlier Digit models, like most industrial robots, operated inside fenced cells to keep people out of reach. Digit 5 is designed to work in the open, using sensors and a separate safety controller that can make it stop, back away or drop into a seated position when a person gets close, according to the company’s hardware rundown from The Robot Report.

The robot stands 5 feet 11 inches tall and weighs 284 pounds, roughly the mass of two adult humans packed into a torso, legs and a pair of articulated arms. That weight matters less as a curiosity than as context for what follows: a machine that heavy needs a battery system that can be recharged fast enough to stay useful across a full shift, and Agility has built its pitch to investors and warehouse customers around exactly that number.

The 90-minute run, nine-minute charge math

Digit 5 runs for about 90 minutes on a charge and returns to full power in roughly 9 minutes, a figure Agility frames as a 10-to-1 run-to-charge ratio, up from the 2-to-1 ratio it says the previous Digit 4 managed, per the company’s own announcement. The idealised arithmetic gives each 99-minute cycle 90 minutes of runtime and nine minutes of charging. Repeating that ratio across 24 hours yields about 21.8 hours of runtime and 2.2 hours of charging before allowing for maintenance, handoffs or faults. Agility is measuring two things and projecting a third. The 90-minute runtime and 9-minute recharge are specifications the company attaches to Digit 5’s battery hardware. The “more than 20 productive hours” figure is a company calculation built from those two hardware numbers, assuming charging cycles that fit cleanly around a robot’s task queue — no downtime, faults or maintenance stops of the kind that show up in real operations. Agility has not published an independent customer-floor validation of a Digit 5 working day yet.

Independent reporting on the launch has generally repeated the 20-hour figure as Agility’s claim rather than as a verified outcome. Alongside the battery changes, Agility increased what Digit 5 can physically do. Agility is not the only company chasing this category, and the comparison is not entirely favorable to Digit 5 on paper. Boston Dynamics’ electric Atlas, per the same Forbes report, is rated to carry up to 66 pounds, reach 7.5 feet and run for about four hours on a hot-swappable battery pack that can be physically pulled and replaced rather than recharged in place. On payload and reach, Atlas currently claims an edge. Digit 5’s advantage is charging speed and, by extension, uptime: a fixed nine-minute recharge cycle is a different operational model than swapping battery packs, and it is the piece Agility is betting its productivity math on.

Orders, a SPAC, and a company still losing money

The timing of the announcement lines up with a corporate transition. Agility disclosed more than $300 million in multi-year customer orders for Digit 5, a figure the company itself qualifies as subject to unspecified contractual milestones being met, and it disclosed the number days after filing paperwork for a SPAC merger with Churchill Capital Corp XI, a deal valued at roughly $2.5 billion. Regulatory filings tied to that merger show a company still far from commercial scale: Agility net sales and losses came to $1.78 million in 2025, up from $310,000 in 2024, against an operating loss of $140.2 million that roughly doubled year over year, and an auditor’s note flagging “substantial doubt” about its ability to continue as a going concern absent further financing.

That financial picture is the backdrop against which the hardware claims should be read; it doesn’t make them false. A company preparing to go public via SPAC has a direct financial incentive to publish its most favorable operating math right before that listing, and the $300 million order figure and 20-hour productivity claim are doing real work in that narrative, alongside more grounded facts, like Amazon’s $1.05 million purchase of five Digit units — a completed transaction, not a pipeline projection.

What 2027 actually promises customers

Agility says early customer access to Digit 5 is expected to begin in the first half of 2027, with general availability, aimed at manufacturing, warehouse and distribution operators, following by the end of that year. The company also plans to extend sales into the European Union and United Kingdom alongside its existing North American base, pending regulatory approval in those markets. Those dates put Digit 5’s actual commercial debut several months out from this week’s unveiling, and every performance figure attached to the robot right now, from its 90-minute runtime to its 20-hour workday, is a specification and a projection. Still, this has not yet been measured on a customer floor.

Estonia’s population stood at 1,360,745 at the start of 2026, according to Statistics Estonia. That is smaller than many single cities. Out of it has come ten companies that reached a billion-dollar valuation at some point in their history, among them Skype, Wise, Bolt, Pipedrive, Playtech and Veriff, according to Invest in Estonia’s own tally.

Using CB Insights’ underlying company data alongside that population figure, a figure Invest in Estonia and outlets including Fintech Baltic put at roughly 7.1 unicorns per million residents, based on Invest in Estonia’s cumulative count of companies that have ever reached $1B — not a live ranking CB Insights itself publishes, second only to Liechtenstein and more than three times the United States’ rate of about 2.2 per million.

The tiger leap that came before the unicorns

This density didn’t happen by accident, and it didn’t start with a startup. In 1996, five years after regaining independence from the Soviet Union, Estonia launched a state programme called Tiigrihüpe, or Tiger Leap, championed by future president Toomas Hendrik Ilves and education minister Jaak Aaviksoo. Its goal was blunt: wire the country’s schools for computers and the internet as a deliberate act of catching up. It worked faster than almost anyone expected.

The rollout was rapid but not instantaneous. Education Estonia says all schools had computers by 2000 and all were connected to the internet by 2001. A per-capita unicorn count says nothing about how many of those companies are still worth a billion dollars today, still headquartered in Estonia, or profitable. For a country with fewer people than a mid-sized American county, that is the more durable claim.

An hour disappears into the phone and the honest inventory afterwards runs to three items: a man cutting marble, somebody’s strong opinion about interest rates, a dog on a skateboard.

None of it is retained in any way worth having. The hour still lands like work.

That mismatch, between the feeling of effort and the absence of anything learned, has a reasonable research explanation behind it, and willpower barely features in it.

A feed is a run of cold starts

Reading a book is one long continuous job. The brain loads a setting, a cast, an argument, and then keeps using that same setup for as long as the reading lasts.

A feed offers nothing of the kind.

Each post arrives with its own subject, tone, format and rules, which means the machinery of attention has to reconfigure itself before any of the content can be processed.

A feed adds another recurring job: a verdict. Each item has to be sized up for whether it is true, whether it is funny, whether it is aimed at anyone in particular. That call gets made before the thing can be dismissed, and then made again at the next one, and the one after that.

Psychologists have taken that reconfiguration apart. In a paper published in the Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance, Joshua Rubinstein, David Meyer and Jeffrey Evans described two stages: goal shifting, meaning the decision to do this now instead of that, and rule activation, meaning the swap of mental instructions from the old job to the new one. Both stages take time. A single switch might cost only a few tenths of a second. That sounds trivial until you count the switches inside an hour of scrolling.

Their experiments used arithmetic and shape-sorting rather than phones, so applying the finding to a feed is an inference, not a measurement.

The part that stays behind

Switching also leaves something on the floor. Sophie Leroy, now a professor at the University of Washington Bothell, coined the term attention residue in a 2009 paper in Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, after experiments in which people were pulled off one task and pushed onto another. Performance on the second task dropped, because a slice of their attention was still parked on the first, and the effect was sharpest when the first task had been left unfinished.

Scrolling has the shape of that setup. Post after post is dropped mid-thought and replaced by the next one, which looks a great deal like the unfinished condition Leroy identified as the costly one. Her participants were working through lab tasks, though. The parallel to a phone is drawn by analogy, and nobody has run the experiment there.

Forty-seven seconds

Gloria Mark, a professor of informatics at the University of California, Irvine, has been logging how long people stay on a single screen since 2004. Back then the average was about two and a half minutes. In an interview with the University of California, she put the recent figure at roughly 47 seconds, with a median of 40, meaning half of all observed stretches were shorter than that.

That number needs handling with care. It is assembled from separate studies across two decades, not one group of people followed the whole way, and what it measures is screen behaviour. People still read long books. They just do it somewhere other than a browser tab.

Why a book behaves differently

Does the medium itself change how much gets understood? Pablo Delgado of the University of Valencia and three co-authors pooled 54 studies covering more than 171,000 participants in a meta-analysis for Educational Research Review, and found a consistent, modest advantage for paper. The gap widened when reading was timed instead of self-paced, held for informational texts but not narrative ones, and grew across the years studied, an unhelpful trend for anyone expecting digital natives to close it.

Pooling dozens of experiments makes that result sturdier than any single study, though the effect itself stays small.

Maryanne Wolf, who studies the reading brain at UCLA, argues in an op-ed for the Guardian that skimming squeezes out the slower processes that make reading useful: drawing inferences, making analogies, testing whether a claim is true, stepping into another person’s point of view. Move the eye fast enough and there is no room left for any of it.

Where the tiredness comes from

Fatigue needs its own explanation, and it comes from a separate strand of Mark’s research.

In a study presented at the 2008 CHI conference, Mark, working with Daniela Gudith and Ulrich Klocke, interrupted people mid-task and measured what happened. The interrupted group finished faster, with no drop in quality, which was the surprise. They also reported more stress, more frustration, more time pressure and more effort.

Compensation, in other words.

The brain appears to cover the cost of fragmentation by spending harder. Mark’s participants were working rather than scrolling, and the equivalent test has not been run on a feed, so the link is suggestive rather than established. Even so, the flatness and irritability at the end of a long scroll, the vague sense of having been mugged, match what those participants described.

Which puts the whole exercise in a different light. An hour on a feed involves several hundred small decisions made at speed, each one demanding a quick ruling on what the thing is and whether it matters. The content was the least of it. The deciding was the job.

Nobody sends an invoice for that. The tiredness is the receipt.

A pair of speakers, two years old, is up for sale online. When no music is playing, they give off an annoying static noise, and the listing does not say so.

A buyer’s message ends with a pointed question: “The speakers don’t have any problems, do they?” In one of the experiments built around that exact question, 85 percent of sellers mentioned the noise, and fewer buyers than that expected their seller to mention a problem.

Shira Garber and three colleagues staged a string of these secondhand sales online across five main studies and a pilot, added a second pilot that surveyed people about what drives negotiators, and reported the results in an open-access paper in Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin this July. Buyers, they found, often underestimated how honest sellers would be. Sellers also reported more concern with being honest, fair and kind, and less concern with the money, than buyers credited them with.

How often did sellers come clean?

In each of the five main studies, some participants played sellers of a secondhand device with a defect they had been told about: an iPod whose battery drained fast, an electric scooter with a faulty battery, the speakers with the static. The rest played buyers, who could earn bonuses for accurately predicting how honest sellers would be.

In the first four studies, a seller counted as honest only if a reply named the defect. Staying quiet counted as dishonest, and so did a dodge like a battery that “isn’t brand new.”

The first pilot set the pattern. Of 76 online workers playing sellers, 63.2 percent picked a truthful opening message over one describing the iPod as being in excellent condition. Of 85 observers given the same information, 43.5 percent predicted the truthful one.

In Study 1, the 176 sellers wrote their own replies to “What can you tell me about it?” and “Anything else?” Of those sellers, 51.7 percent disclosed the battery problem, while the 270 buyers guessed, on average, that 43.2 percent would. With the scooter and a direct question in Study 2, three quarters of sellers disclosed the fault.

The rate swung with the setup. One cause, a direct question, got its own test; other swings the researchers could not fully explain. Until the last study, the exchanges were also largely scripted, with sellers answering pre-written buyer messages rather than a live counterpart.

The way the question is asked

Study 3, with 483 participants, gave half the sellers the pointed “The speakers don’t have any problems, do they?” and half the open “What can you tell me about them?” Buyers here were not told about the static, which is closer to how a real listing works.

The direct question made sellers more likely to mention the noise. Buyers’ predictions did not move with it.

The gap between expected and actual honesty was statistically significant under the direct question and not under the open one, so even inside this paper it did not show up everywhere. Of several possible reasons Study 1 still found a gap with open questions, the authors single out one: sellers there had two chances to come clean, and concealing twice may weigh more on a seller’s conscience than concealing once.

A few minutes of small talk

Study 5 was the only one that paired people live. It matched 422 participants into 211 buyer-seller pairs on an online platform, and some pairs first spent three minutes chatting about something they had enjoyed recently or how they unwind after a busy day.

Across the study, buyers rated their seller’s likely honesty at 6.56 on a ten-point scale, while coders scored the sellers’ actual replies at 7.51. Among pairs who chatted first, that difference was no longer statistically significant. Sellers’ scores did not differ significantly between the two conditions. The chat raised buyers’ expectations of honesty instead.

Study 4 tried a different nudge on 358 participants. Some buyers were asked about the seller’s moral concerns before predicting, others afterward. Thinking about the seller’s conscience first raised buyers’ expectations, and the gap was nearly halved.

It did not close. The authors suggest one reason: 85 percent of sellers in that study disclosed, a rate higher than in the matching condition of Study 3 for reasons they say are not readily apparent.

Where the suspicion comes from

Study 2 measured three motives, adding the pull of money to the two that Study 1 had tracked. The 214 management undergraduates who took part rated, on a seven-point scale, how much the seller had been weighing being decent, feeling guilty, and getting the best price. Sellers put their concern with being a decent person at 4.99, and buyers guessed 3.78. Buyers put the seller’s interest in money at 6.03; sellers reported 5.06.

The sellers still cared about the money. They cared about it less, and about their own decency more, than the buyers pictured.

The paper’s explanation leans on moral typecasting, the idea that people tend to see others as either doers or feelers, rarely both. A seller holds the object and the information, so, the authors argue, a buyer casts them as a doer, and the competitive setting makes that doer look like someone chasing an advantage rather than guarding a clean conscience. In the abstract’s words: “While sellers tended to be honest because of moral identity concerns, buyers expected them to be driven primarily by self-interest.”

Two duller explanations get a hearing too, and the authors say their own mechanism is not the only one. Poor forecasting in general, they point out, gives no reason to expect guesses to run low rather than high. Plain caution, a buyer bracing for the worst to avoid a loss, gets mixed treatment: the Study 4 discussion offers it as a possible added force, while the general discussion says it cannot explain the results, because in the first pilot observers with nothing at stake still underestimated the sellers.

Their mediation analyses deserve a lighter touch than the abstract’s sentence suggests. Buyers and sellers answered parallel versions of the motive questions rather than the same ones, and the authors say the results should be “cautiously interpreted” for that reason. Sellers rated their motives after choosing whether to disclose, which leaves room for a flattering story told afterward, though the authors argue buyers’ parallel ratings may reduce that concern. And in Study 1, the measure of anticipated guilt and related feelings showed no significant difference between buyers and sellers.

Small stakes, narrow scope

The stakes stayed small. Most bonuses were paid by lottery, and a seller in Study 1 had a five percent chance of earning at most $7. The authors grant that low stakes may keep self-interest from fully switching on, while citing earlier work that finds self-interest at work even when stakes are small.

The honesty studied was one kind: telling a buyer about a defect the seller knew. Misrepresenting a bottom price or inventing urgency, both named by the authors, were outside the design. They describe the findings as “based primarily on Western participant samples,” and the sales were one-off exchanges between strangers, chosen to keep reputation largely out of play. Ongoing work relationships and repeat customers sit outside what was measured.

Suspicion is sometimes the sensible response, and the paper says so. A buyer facing a salesperson expected to use persuasion tactics, or shopping where one side knows far more than the other, as with used cars, has good reason for care. The paper does not argue for trusting everyone. It asks for work on when doubting a counterpart’s honesty hurts a negotiator and when it protects one.

Every finding in this piece comes from the published text and tables of one paper, read by an editorial desk that reports on research and does not train negotiators; the supplementary files the paper points to could not be opened. The studies compared predictions with replies across hundreds of people, which says something about buyers and sellers like the ones studied, taken as groups, and cannot tell anyone whether the particular seller in their inbox is being straight with them. For a purchase that matters, sensible safeguards include an independent inspection, a written description of the item’s condition, and the buyer protection some platforms offer.

This paper did not measure what the gap costs. The authors’ illustration is a used car that looks too good to be true, and a buyer who distrusts the seller, walks away, and settles for something worse. Examining what the honesty gap does to the outcomes of negotiations is what they call an important next step; they also call for testing the idea where far more money is at stake.

The difference between performing politeness for authority and treating service workers as fully human often comes down to lessons learned before you could remember them.]]>

Every restaurant service contains a half-second that gives the whole game away. A plate lands. The customer looks up at whoever carried it and says thanks, or looks straight through them and carries on talking.

Nobody is scoring it. Nobody remembers it an hour later. And yet the reflex tends to have a long history behind it, much of it laid down years earlier by an adult asking one small, maddening question at exactly the wrong moment.

The magic word was never magic

Spend an afternoon near a toddler and the routine is unmissable. Someone offers a biscuit, the kid grabs it and turns to leave, and a parent says: what do you say?

Linguists have sat down and measured this. A 1980 study in the journal Language in Society watched 22 children and their parents at play, then sent an assistant in with a gift. Unprompted, the children rarely produced these little courtesies, and thank you was the scarcest of the three. What did happen was prompting. Parents nudged, the children almost always complied, and they parroted the adult’s phrasing exactly.

One detail is easy to skip past. Parents used the routines themselves, in front of the child. Mothers more than fathers. The study measured that behaviour without testing its effects, but it is hard to watch a parent thank a stranger a thousand times and come away with nothing.

So that reflexive thanks nobody thinks about? This is one place it can begin. Hundreds of tiny repetitions, every one long forgotten, are the sort of thing that builds a habit able to fire before conscious thought does.

Who actually says thank you

This is where the usual class assumptions wobble. A 1986 study of 250 preschoolers tested what children did with no parent in the room. Around 37 per cent said thank you spontaneously when handed a reward. Children from low-income families did so more often than those from middle-income families.

Worth holding that one loosely. It is a single study, forty years old, run in one country, and income is a crude proxy for a great deal else. Still, it dents the comfortable assumption that manners arrive bundled with money.

The people who can do nothing for you

Anyone who has run a dining room knows the tell. How a guest talks to the owner reveals almost nothing, because that exchange is a performance. The reading comes later, when the seventeen-year-old arrives to clear the plates and nobody important is watching.

Some people adjust their voice. It goes flatter, clipped, faintly impatient, then swings back up the moment a manager appears. Others do not change at all. Same warmth for the kid with the tray as for the owner, because nobody told them there were two settings.

Where does that second group come from? No research trails those adults back to their childhoods, so this next bit is a hunch rather than a finding.

The hunch: they grew up in houses where courtesy went to everyone who came through the door. The plumber got offered a drink. The delivery driver got thanked by name. Nobody sat the children down and explained a value system. They watched it happen a few thousand times.

Does it matter who gets it?

A reasonable objection: surely kindness shown to people you love matters more than kindness shown to whoever hands over your coffee.

Researchers put that to the test. A 2019 experiment with 683 participants had people spend a week performing deliberate acts of kindness. One group directed them at close friends and family, one at weak ties and strangers, one at themselves, and a fourth just watched for kindness around them. A control group did nothing.

Every kindness group got happier than the controls, and the more acts people performed, the bigger the lift. No group pulled ahead of the others.

Two things to flag before anyone runs with that. It was a short study measuring self-reported happiness. And an act of kindness performed because a researcher asked for it is a long way from an unthinking thank you at a coffee counter. The study was not built to measure everyday courtesy and cannot settle anything about it.

What it does suggest is that closeness to the recipient mattered far less than most people would guess. Whether that holds for the small automatic stuff is an open question.

Small things that shift it

None of this requires a personality transplant. Four places to start:

  • Get names. Baristas, security guards, cleaners, the guy at the corner shop. Ask once, use it forever.
  • Thank people for work, not just favours. Someone doing the job they are paid for still did something for you.
  • Watch for the voice switch. Most people who have one are unaware of it.
  • If there are kids around, demonstrate instead of explaining. They are reading the room, not the lecture.

An unthinking please earns its owner remarkably little credit. It costs nothing and takes no effort, which is rather the point. Someone put the work in years ago so that it would not have to be a decision.

]]> Quote of the day: “Sometimes you find yourself in the middle of nowhere, and sometimes, in the middle of nowhere, you find yourself” https://siliconcanals.com/d-quote-of-the-day-sometimes-you-find-yourself-in-the-middle-of-nowhere-and-sometimes-in-the-middle-of-nowhere-you-find-yourself/ Thu, 17 Sep 2026 10:45:39 +0000 https://siliconcanals.com/?p=109380

What happens when your plans collapse, your phone dies, and you're stranded at a gas station thousands of miles from home—and it's the best thing that could've happened.]]>

The last time I was properly lost, I was standing at a petrol station somewhere north of Chiang Rai with a dead phone, a warm bottle of water and a dog who clearly ran the place. My bus had left without me. I had four hours to wait, nothing to do and no way to tell anyone about it.

It was the calmest I had been in about eighteen months.

Sometimes you find yourself in the middle of nowhere, and sometimes, in the middle of nowhere, you find yourself.

Yes, it is the sort of line that ends up engraved on a bracelet and screwed to somebody’s kitchen wall. Both of which have happened, it turns out. I went looking for whoever wrote it and found nothing, only evidence that it has been circulating since at least 2014 with no author attached. Anonymous, then. It holds up better than most things sold at a craft market.

Nowhere is mostly an absence of audience

Here is what I think the line is really about. Nowhere has very little to do with distance. It is any situation where nobody knows your job title.

In a city you are surrounded by people who already have a version of you loaded. The neighbour who thinks you are the loud one. The old colleague who still introduces you by the thing you did in 2019. You end up performing that version without noticing, because it is easier than correcting everybody.

Take the audience away and something odd happens. For a day or two you feel faintly useless, because nobody needs anything from you. Then the noise drops. You start hearing your own opinions, which are less impressive and a good deal more honest than the ones you say out loud.

That is the whole mechanism. No mysticism required.

The year my diary went blank

I lost my business, restaurants, during the pandemic. The deal was agreed over a phone call while I sat on a plastic chair in a dining room with the lights off, and it was the least bad option available to me at the time.

For years my day had been decided for me by suppliers, staff rotas and the seven o’clock rush. Then it was not. I woke up on a Tuesday with an empty calendar and genuinely no idea what a Tuesday was for.

I would love to tell you this was peaceful. I reorganised the same cupboard twice. I developed strong opinions about a neighbour’s parking. I rang people I had not spoken to in five years and could hear them wondering what I wanted.

The useful part arrived about three months in, once I had run out of things to tidy. With no restaurant to point at, I had to work out what I would actually do with a day if nobody was paying me for it. The answer was writing, which was inconvenient, as it pays considerably worse than a burger.

You can get lost for the price of a bus ticket

You do not need to sell a business or fly to Patagonia. Nowhere comes in small doses and most of them are free.

Pick a district of your own city you have no reason to visit and spend three hours there on foot. Not a famous one. A dull one, with hardware shops and a wet market and nothing on sale to anyone carrying a suitcase. I do this in Bangkok about once a month and I have never regretted it, though I have frequently regretted the shoes.

Go somewhere your phone cannot help you. Not switched off, just outgunned: the lanes are not on the map and the only language on offer is one you do not speak.

Be a beginner at something in public. Take a class where you are visibly the worst person in the room. It is physically uncomfortable for about twenty minutes. After that it stops mattering, and what is left is quite close to fun.

And if you do travel, leave one day entirely unplanned. No booking, no list, no reservation you have to walk fast to reach. Most people schedule a trip so tightly that they never get further than a warmer version of their normal week.

What actually turns up

Let me manage expectations. You do not come back from a petrol station with a revelation.

What you come back with is a shorter list. Two or three things you thought you cared about turn out to belong to somebody else. One or two things you have never mentioned to anyone are suddenly all you think about when there is nothing else to think about. That is it. It looks like very little on paper. It does not feel that way at thirty-eight, when you are still doing a job you picked at twenty-two to impress someone who stopped watching years ago.

There is a trap in this, though. Some people use the middle of nowhere as somewhere to hide, and the giveaway is that they keep having to go back. If every trip is an escape from the same unaddressed thing at home, the scenery is doing the work of a conversation you have been avoiding. Distance is excellent for seeing a problem clearly. It has never once solved one for me.

The dog at the petrol station, for the record, took no interest in any of this. He sat under the ice cabinet, moved twice in four hours, and had evidently worked something out about Wednesdays that I am still catching up on.

]]>

CMR Surgical said it designed Versius to be compact and modular, so it doesn’t require a dedicated OR. | Source: CMR Surgical

Stryker this week said it has invested about $400 million into CMR Surgical, with an exclusive option for it to acquire the company’s remaining equity. Stryker also secured an exclusive U.S. commercial agency agreement for the Versius portfolio.

“This strategic alliance is a significant milestone for CMR and a strong endorsement of the technology, clinical experience, and global business we have built,” stated Massimiliano Colella, CEO of CMR Surgical. “Stryker’s investment will give us additional strength to accelerate innovation and the continued global expansion of the Versius portfolio, while its scale and deep customer relationships create a significant growth opportunity in the United States.”

Cambridge, U.K.-based CMR Surgical said it has designed the Versius platform for real-world operating environments. The surgical robot‘s modular architecture supports flexibility across procedures, surgeon access and sites of care, the company claimed.

CMR Surgical gets clearance for more procedures

CMR Surgical said that Versius can help healthcare providers grow robotic adoption within existing operating room workflows. This scalable approach can help health systems meet growing demand for robotic-assisted surgery while preserving operational flexibility and supporting long-term program economics, added the company.

Versius supports procedures including general surgery, colorectal surgery, urology, gynecology and thoracic surgery. The robot has has been adopted in hospitals across more than 30 countries and used in 45,000 cases worldwide, according to CMR.

The Versius Plus system has earned FDA 510(k) clearance for cholecystectomy. CMR has also filed a 510(k) submission for benign gynecological indications. The robot has been used in 45,000 cases worldwide, it said.

Stryker to sell Versius system in the U.S.

“Soft-tissue robotics is a high-growth adjacency and a natural extension of Stryker’s strengths in endoscopy, visualization, and enabling technologies,” stated Andy Pierce, the group president of medsurg and neurotechnology at Stryker.

“We have evaluated the segment carefully for years, and this alliance represents a thoughtful and disciplined entry that combines the complementary strengths of both companies,” he added. “We selected CMR Surgical and the Versius portfolio because of the opportunity to help healthcare providers grow robotic-assisted surgery adoption across a broad range of procedures in hospitals and ASCs.”

“We also look forward to welcoming Andy Pierce to our board of directors and benefiting from his more than 30 years of MedTech leadership experience at Stryker as we continue expanding access to robotic-assisted surgery globally,” said Colella.

Moving forward, Stryker will serve as the exclusive U.S. sales agent for the Versius portfolio, while CMR Surgical will continue to lead portfolio development and commercialization in markets outside the United States.

Stryker’s exclusive acquisition option gives it the option of buying 100% of CMR Surgical’s outstanding equity in the future, subject to the agreement’s terms. This transaction is subject to regulatory approvals and customary closing conditions.

The ADI cleanroom in Beaverton, Ore.

Sponsored by Analog Devices Inc.

Robotics companies are developing new capabilities at a rapid pace, from autonomous mobile robots to humanoid systems. However, keeping up with technological advances is one part of the challenge. The most critical thing is to turn a successful prototype into a commercially viable product that can be manufactured and deployed at scale. 

“The biggest challenge I see robotics startups facing today is the speed at which the industry moves,” says Cameron Villone, Senior Product Technology Manager at Analog Devices Inc. (ADI). 

In most cases, a startup excels in adopting next-generation technologies in sensing, motion control, and AI, but commercialization requires additional expertise in electronics, system integration, validation, and manufacturing. These demands can often stretch the resources of smaller engineering teams. 

ADI is developing its Emerging Tech Hub within the Analog Garage to help robotics startups and established companies overcome these challenges. The Emerging Tech Hub is intended to give companies access to ADI engineers, prototyping and testing resources, and manufacturing and sourcing expertise as they prepare their designs for production. 

The challenges of scaling robotics innovation 

ADI was recently highlighted in The Race to Make AI Physical whitepaper explaining how physical AI brings together sensing, signal conversion, perception, reasoning, control, computing, and validation. These functions must work together for a robot to perform reliably. Even when a robot makes the right decision, executing that decision depends on accurate sensor data, timely control signals, and sufficient power to drive its actuators. 

These engineering requirements continue to change as the product progresses from prototype to production. For example, a prototype needs to demonstrate whether technology can work, but commercialization requires the complete system to perform consistently under different operating conditions. 

ADI describes this through four stages: Idea, Prototype, Validate, and Scale. The initial stages focus on developing and demonstrating the concept, while validation involves testing the integrated system, identifying potential problems, and optimizing the design before production. Scaling introduces additional manufacturing and supply chain requirements. 

Robotics companies need to secure components, coordinate production, and maintain consistent quality as volumes increase. “ADI’s expansive experience in sensor development and semiconductor manufacturing allows for knowledge-driven support when these robotic developers move from idea to production,” says Villone. 

These changing demands for a robotics startup are the gaps ADI’s Emerging Tech Hub is intended to address. 

The Emerging Tech Hub brings expertise and resources 

The Emerging Tech Hub is a robotics-focused initiative being developed to bring startups and established robotics companies closer to ADI’s technical teams, including engineers implementing newly released or still-in-development technologies. 

Villone describes the approach as “co-development,” where when a company approaches the Emerging Tech Hub, the first step is to establish their current capabilities, what they are trying to achieve, and how to alginalign these goals with the Emerging Tech Hub’s mission. From there, the two sides can determine what kind of collaboration is appropriate. 

The engineering support from ADI will depend on the robotics company’s stage and needs. For example, a mature robotics developer might need a particular semiconductor component, while another may be trying to solve a different engineering problem, prompting the Emerging Tech Hub to find specialists within ADI. An early-stage startup might need broader guidance to clarify its architecture and identify what further development requires. 

The Emerging Tech Hub brings three areas of support together. The technical expertise ranges from robotics, control, edge AI, power, and system integration. Development resources include laboratories, prototyping tools, reference designs, testing and validation capabilities, and hands-on engineering support. For companies preparing to increase production, it also provides sourcing guidance and industry connections. 

Villone said ADI has recruited robotics experts from across the industry to be better equipped to handle fast paced robotic development. He cited ADI’s GMSL technology as one example of expertise that can help robotics developers address camera connectivity and integration. This support extends beyond simply component selection to decisions about how technologies fit within the wider robotic system. 

The Emerging Tech Hub is still being prepared for wider external participation, with applications expected to open by the end of 2026. 

Bridging startup agility and corporate resources 

Startups need flexibility to test ideas quickly and retain control of their technology. But working with a large technology company can introduce a tension between speed and structure. 

Villone acknowledged that some startups are reluctant to work with larger corporations because they worry about what such a relationship could mean for their business. However, he sees an opportunity when the intentions are clear. 

ADI’s interest is in enabling robotics applications using its semiconductors, while startups can benefit from expertise and resources that would be difficult to develop independently. The partnership works best when both sides understand what they want to accomplish. 

This is the same model ADI is proposing for its Emerging Tech Hub. The company describes the relationship as collaborative, with flexible, startup-friendly engagement, with the and startups retaining their intellectual property. These principles allow companies to seek technical support without surrendering ownership of their innovations. 

The same questions will be explored at RoboBusiness on October 20 during “Robotics Startup Boot Camp Part 2: Challenges & Best Practices for Working with Corporate Partners.” 

Colm Prendergast, senior director and head of the Emerging Tech Hub at ADI, will join representatives from MassRobotics and WiBotic to discuss how startups can pursue proofs of concept and pilots, how corporations evaluate potential partners, and how startup agility can coexist with corporate processes. 

The discussion aims to make those relationships more practical for companies preparing to commercialize their technologies. 

Conclusion 

A robotics company requires engineering expertise, system validation, production planning, reliable component sourcing, and industry partnerships to successfully bring the innovation to market. ADI’s Emerging Tech Hub addresses these challenges by connecting robotics companies with technical expertise and development resources. 

To learn more about building successful corporate partnerships, attend Robotics Startup Boot Camp Part 2 at RoboBusiness, where industry leaders will discuss the opportunities and challenges of working together. Register now to attend.

What does your humanoid robot’s motion system need to do?

For engineers developing humanoids, the answer involves balancing torque, speed, stiffness, weight, positioning accuracy, and available space. Each joint presents its own requirements, and the right solution begins with understanding those demands.

That is the approach behind Timken Precision Drives, part of The Timken Co. Bringing together Cone Drive, SPINEA, CGI Motion, and Timken Encoders, the platform combines specialized engineering expertise and complementary technologies to help customers solve their motion control challenges.

The conversation starts with the application: What motion is required? What loads must the system support? Where is the current design falling short? And what needs to change to achieve the desired performance?

Timken engineers around the application

Developers of humanoids face different challenges across load-bearing joints, compact wrists, end effectors, and other moving assemblies. A system that meets the needs of one mechanism may require a different approach elsewhere in the robot.

Timken Precision Drives said it works with customers to evaluate those requirements and identify an appropriate path forward. That may involve a standard component, a modified design, or a custom solution that brings multiple technologies together.

Understanding the application early allows engineering teams to consider how gearing, motors, bearings, and position feedback will interact within the available space. It also helps guide decisions about reduction ratio, load capacity, allowable deflection, duty cycle, and service life.

Complementary technologies, custom possibilities

Timken said its platform’s breadth gives engineers multiple ways to approach a motion challenge.

Cone Drive contributes strain wave gearing expertise for applications requiring compact packaging, high torque density, and zero-backlash positioning. Component and housed configurations provide a foundation for application-specific designs, with opportunities to explore further integration based on customer requirements.

SPINEA brings cycloidal gearing and integrated actuation expertise. TwinSpin reducers and DriveSpin servo actuators offer options for applications where torsional stiffness, torque transmission, and load-handling capability are important design considerations.

CGI Motion adds precision planetary and micro gearing, along with custom design and manufacturing capabilities for compact mechanisms. That expertise supports the exploration of motion solutions where size, configuration, and performance requirements call for a tailored approach.

Timken Encoders complements the mechanical portfolio with magnetic position feedback technologies, including absolute and incremental options.

Timken Precision Drives said these combined capabilities enable it to look across technologies as it works with customers to develop solutions around their specific motion requirements.

NYSOFA established its first public-private partnership in 2018, following a report by AARP and the U.S. Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) on the impact of loneliness and social isolation on older adults and Medicare spending. It stated that loneliness and isolation are equivalent to smoking almost a pack of cigarettes per day, cost Medicare more than $7 billion to treat, and make chronic conditions worse. In addition to its partnership with NYSOFA, Intuition Robotics has similar partnerships in Wisconsin, Florida, and Washington. In Washington, the program is aimed at Medicaid recipients. The Ramat Gan, Israel-based company was founded in 2016.

“Perhaps most importantly, the partnership has reinforced that effective AI companionship isn’t just about answering questions or providing reminders.   • Every month, 88% of participants engage in two-way conversations with ElliQ, 92% regularly share updates about their wellbeing, and 81% participate in physical activity encouraged by ElliQ.
  • 88% of users find that ElliQ has both improved their life for the better and their quality of life.

“This partnership extension continues our long term partnership with the state of New York, and its Office for the Aging, reflecting three years of measurable, record-breaking engagement results: older adults across New York are engaging with ElliQ more often, feeling less lonely, and staying more connected to the people who matter to them,” said Dor Skuler, co-founder and CEO of Intuition Robotics.

“What we have seen is that an AI companion who remembers the older adult, checks in every morning, and encourages them to take a walk or call their daughter can meaningfully change how connected and independent someone feels,” he added. “That is the outcome New York continues to invest in.”
